CHAPTER 4
Environmental Element

INTRODUCTION
Clark County contains a diverse mixture of natural resources, parklands and open spaces. Of the
county’s 656 square miles, almost half is in forest and agricultural lands. Air, water and land
resources are essential to the very existence of human development. They inﬂuence every aspect
of quality of life, from the local climate to the availability of safe drinking water to ﬂood control
and drainage patterns to recreational opportunities and to the habitat that we share with plants
and animals.

The Environmental Element provides speciﬁc environmental goals and requirements as the basis
for development regulations and general goals for land use planning and parks acquisition. The
Environmental Element addresses land development throughout the entire unincorporated area
of the county and includes various environmental policies that apply to the entire county.

RELATIONSHIP OF THE ENVIRONMENTAL ELEMENT
TO OTHER ELEMENTS & PLANS
The Growth Management Act (GMA) recognizes that environmental protection is important to
the citizens of the State of Washington. The GMA contains ﬁve goals that relate to the natural
environment:

   •   Environment. This goal requires protection and enhancement of the environment and of
       the state's high quality of life, including air and water quality, and the availability of water.
   •   Open Space and Recreation. This goal requires the retention of open space and green
       space, the enhancement of recreational opportunities and ﬁsh and wildlife habitat,
       increasing access to natural resource lands and water, and the development of parks and
       recreation facilities. (See Chapter 7 for a more complete discussion of county parks,
       recreation and open space.)
   •   Natural Resource Industries. This goal requires the maintenance and enhancement of
       natural resource-based industries, including productive timber, agricultural and ﬁsheries
       industries. The conservation of productive forest lands and productive agricultural lands is
       encouraged, while incompatible uses are discouraged. (See Chapter 3 for a more complete
       discussion of the county’s natural resource industries.)
   •   Climate Change and Resiliency. This goal ensures that comprehensive plans, development
       regulations, and regional policies, plans, and strategies for countywide planning policies
       and regional transportation planning organizations adapt to and mitigate the effects of a



135                                                                      E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
       changing climate; support reductions in greenhouse gas emissions and per capita vehicle
       miles traveled; prepare for climate impact scenarios; foster resiliency to climate impacts
       and natural hazards; protect and enhance environmental, economic, and human health and
       safety; and advance environmental justice. (See Chapter 14 for a more complete
       discussion of county climate change and resiliency.)
   •   Shorelines of the State. This goal requires the goals and policies of the Shoreline
       Management Act be considered an element of the county’s comprehensive plan. (See
       Chapter 13 for a more complete discussion of the county’s Shoreline Master Program.)

All development activities create some level of impact on the air, water and land resources of the
county. The beneﬁts of development activities are easily measured in terms of economic beneﬁts
to the county or its cities. However, there are often unintended consequences of development
that are not included in the environmental balance sheet, and often include negative impacts to
the public’s ﬁsh and wildlife resources. The programs and policies in the Environmental Element
attempt to address and mitigate these consequences.

The ultimate goal is to recognize the functions and values of the natural environment around us
and to, at a minimum, maintain or improve those functions and values, independent of the type of
development that is proposed. The Environmental Element of the 20-Year Plan is important
because protection and enhancement of our environment has the potential to conﬂict with other
20-Year Plan elements.

ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS & CONSERVATION
PROGRAMS

C R I T IC A L A R E A S
The GMA speciﬁcally lists ﬁve “critical areas” for which local governments must designate and
develop protection and enhancement programs. These are ﬁsh and wildlife habitat, wetlands,
aquifer recharge areas, ﬂood hazard areas and geological hazard areas. Protection of critical areas
and natural resource lands is a key goal and purpose of the GMA and is a longstanding goal of the
Clark County community. The county contains a variety of critical areas, ranging in size and scope
from smaller, discrete areas to broad areas. Fish and wildlife habitat areas provide habitat for
threatened, sensitive or endangered wildlife species. Aquifer recharge areas encompass most of
the lowland area within the county. The soils and terrain create signiﬁcant environmentally
sensitive areas, such as steep, erodible slopes, wetlands and ground water recharge areas (Figure
1). Many types of critical areas geographically overlap.

The beneﬁts that these critical areas yield range from providing ﬁsh, wildlife, or vegetative
ecosystem habitat to limiting or mitigating human concerns over water pollution, ﬂood hazards,
and temperature. Vegetation protection and enhancement is critical to protecting streams and
riparian habitat necessary for sustaining healthy ﬁsh and wildlife populations. Critical areas also


E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                          136
                                      CLARK2045
provide the beneﬁts of recreation, aesthetic enjoyment and water supplies. Maintenance of tree
cover, natural vegetation and wetlands are critical to prevention of erosion, ﬂooding, property and
habitat damage, the continued functioning of the ecosystem and preservation of rural character.

Unlike residential, commercial, industrial, or other uses, critical areas do not constitute a separate
20-Year Plan or zoning designation, unless they are under public ownership. Policies and programs
used to protect and conserve these areas involve a range of federal, state and local programs and
standards. Most policies used to address critical areas are therefore regulatory or incentive-based
and are applied to privately held lands.

One effective way of protecting critical lands is through public ownership. Publicly owned lands
within the urban area are largely conﬁned to parks which emphasize recreational opportunities.
Outside urban areas, most publicly owned lands emphasize wildlife and other critical land values,
although access and passive recreation may be allowed. Protecting sensitive lands through public
ownership requires that substantial funds be raised for acquisition and maintenance of the land.

Prohibitions or limitations on structural development also provide critical lands protection. Such
programs currently in place in Clark County include the Shoreline Master Program; ﬂood hazard,
wetlands and ﬁsh and wildlife conservation areas ordinances; and prohibitions against placement
of structures within designated unstable slope areas. As part of the development review process,
the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) authorizes the imposition of a wide range of conditions
which can prohibit or limit construction within certain areas or enact other mitigation measures to
protect or offset impacts to environmentally sensitive areas.


F I S H & W IL DL I F E H A B I T A T
Most of the land and water area of Clark County provides some form of ﬁsh or wildlife habitat.
Much of this area is in park land, resource production, or open space. Clark County has several
hundred miles of streams and rivers. Under state and federal law, these streams are designated to
support a wide range of “beneﬁcial uses” that include water supplies, support for Endangered
Species Act (ESA) listed species, ﬁsh and wildlife habitat and recreation. The ability of these
streams to meet these beneﬁcial uses is more generally considered stream health. Stream health
has not been comprehensively measured for all streams in the county and much of this work is
underway but not yet complete. Stream health is actively monitored by Clark County Public
Works Clean Water Division, conducting routine or periodic monitoring at most streams in
unincorporated Clark County. Available data on stream health shows that streams range from
near pristine conditions in remote areas of the Cascade Foothills to fair to poor health in urban
areas. Most rural streams could be categorized as being in fair to good health.

There are few lakes in Clark County. Aside from small manmade ponds and seasonal wetland
ponds, the only signiﬁcant lakes within or bordering the county are Vancouver Lake, Battle Ground
Lake, Lacamas Lake, Round Lake, Green Lake, Lake Rosannah, Lake Merwin and Yale Lake. These



137                                                                    E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                       CLARK2045
areas provide essential habitat for a variety of ﬁsh, wildlife and plant species. They also provide
multiple recreation opportunities that include boating, ﬁshing, hunting and wildlife viewing.

Fish species inhabiting the Lower Columbia River, including its tributaries, include both resident
and migratory life history patterns. Resident ﬁsh species generally inhabit the lower Columbia
River their entire lives, where some may travel many miles both intra- and inter- annually. These
species can include resident rainbow trout, cutthroat trout and many non-game species. Migratory
ﬁsh species are considered anadromous, and include salmon, steelhead, and sturgeon.
Anadromous ﬁsh hatch in freshwater, migrate to the ocean as fry or parr where they mature over a
period of years, and return to freshwater to spawn. In addition to critical areas, the GMA requires
that local jurisdictions address the requirements of anadromous ﬁsh species.

Certain areas of important habitat are readily identiﬁable because of their protected status under
public ownership. The US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) Ridgeﬁeld National Wildlife Refuge
contains over 5,000 acres of Columbia River ﬂoodplain consisting of marshes, lakes, woodlands,
grasslands and croplands, which provide migration and wintering habitat for Paciﬁc Flyway
waterfowl, as well as many species of water birds, raptors, shore and songbirds. The concentration
and diversity of native and migratory bird species in the Refuge are the largest in the county; and
includes sandhill cranes, a state endangered species. Several species of mammals, reptiles and
amphibians can also be found in the Refuge, including Columbian white-tailed deer, a state and
federally threatened species.

USFWS Steigerwald Lake National Wildlife Refuge, located in the southeast corner of the county,
includes 627 acres of Columbia River bottomland, consisting of reed canary grass marshes,
riparian woodlands and improved pastures. Among the species inhabiting the Refuge are raptors,
geese and marsh, water and riparian woodland songbirds. The Vancouver Lake lowlands area
provides over 1,000 acres of wildlife habitat within close proximity to Vancouver. The Washington
State Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) owns and manages approximately 2,400 acres as
the Shillapoo Wildlife Area. The wildlife area provides habitat to wintering waterfowl, neotropical
migratory birds, Columbia white-tailed deer and contains a mix of agriculture lands, developed
pastures, wetlands, and oak woodlands.

Wildlife habitat is not restricted to those areas already under public ownership. Agricultural and
forest lands designated as resource lands under the GMA play a crucial role in providing important
wildlife habitat, such as winter-feeding areas, wildlife movement corridors, and buffers from more
intense development. Effective habitat connectivity requires strategic planning that goes beyond
jurisdictional boundaries. Landscape-scale land use planning can help mitigate habitat loss by
preserving large blocks of native habitat and protecting natural corridors – such as river forest
corridors and ridgetops – that link these remaining habitat areas. This approach is essential for
maintaining biodiversity and facilitating animal movement.




E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                           138
                                      CLARK2045
Through the Priority Habitat and Species (PHS) program, WDFW collects and analyzes data on
priority species and habitats, offering maps, lists and management recommendations that,
together, are essential for the designation and protection of Fish and Wildlife Habitat
Conservation Areas. This data can guide land use planning efforts and help ensure that critical
habitats are preserved and properly managed (Figure 2).


F I S H & W IL DL I F E H A B I T A T C O N SE R V A T I O N P R O GR A M S
The county’s ﬁsh and wildlife conservation areas ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.445) was adopted in
1997 and signiﬁcantly updated in 2006 and 2023. The stated purpose of the ordinance is to:
further the goal of no net loss of habitat functions and values within designated habitat areas by
protecting environmentally distinct, fragile and valuable ﬁsh and wildlife habitat areas for present
and future generations, while also allowing for reasonable use of private property. This ordinance
intends to conserve the functional integrity of the habitats needed to perpetually support ﬁsh and
wildlife populations.

The county most recently updated the ordinance in 2023 to reﬂect the best available information
as required by the GMA and has continued to update the ordinance as needed to remain
consistent with the new guidance from the Washington Department of Fish & Wildlife (WDFW)
and Washington Department of Commerce (Commerce). Development proposals involving
impacts to priority habitats and species often require consultation with WDFW.


H A B I T A T C O N S ER V A T I O N B A N K IN G
Habitat conservation banking is a method of mitigating a decrease in or loss of habitat function by
providing habitat functions and values (e.g. creating, restoring, enhancing and/or protecting
wetlands) away from the site of a proposed development project. A habitat conservation bank
generates credits that can be used for habitat mitigation for individual projects with ﬁsh and
wildlife habitat conservation area impacts. Conservation banking has a number of beneﬁts over
other mitigation strategies including:

   •   consolidation of small isolated mitigation projects into larger, more ecologically signiﬁcant
       sites;
   •   higher likelihood of long-term mitigation success; and,
   •   efﬁciency in permit review for projects using bank credits.

Habitat conservation banking is not a means of reducing the protection and conservation of
wetlands in the urban area. It is only a method to improve mitigation success at a regional scale
and streamline permit review for projects that have habitat impacts. The criteria used to evaluate
and permit habitat impacts are independent of the type of mitigation proposed and, instead, focus
on the beneﬁts and design of the project. A key element to developing an effective habitat
conservation banking program is to maintain a good inventory of high functioning habitat areas
that are at risk of habitat degradation in order to allow conservation bank developers to locate


139                                                                   E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                       CLARK2045
sites that are well suited to bank development. Another key element is to ensure that the habitat
permitting process gives due consideration to the use of conservation bank credits when they are
available. Clark County has a process for authorizing conservation banks and administers two
Oregon White Oak Woodland Conservation banks.


E N D AN G E R E D S P E C I E S A C T
The United States Congress passed the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in 1973. It establishes
various processes and programs targeting conservation and recovery of species that are listed as
threatened or endangered. Clark County supports multiple ﬁsh species listed as threatened under
the ESA, including Chinook (listed 1999), Coho (listed 2005), chum salmon (listed 1999), steelhead
(listed 1998), bull trout (listed 1999), eulachon (listed 2010), and green sturgeon (listed 2006).

Clark County also has populations of, or the potential for, other important ﬁsh and wildlife species
listed under the Federal ESA. These species include gray wolf (listed in 1974), Columbian white-
tail deer (listed in 1968), northern spotted owl (listed in 1990), streaked horned lark (listed in
2013), yellow-billed cuckoo (listed in 1997), Oregon spotted frog (listed in 2014), golden
paintbrush (listed in 1997), water howelia (listed in 1994), Fender’s blue butterﬂy (2000) and
Kincaid’s lupine (2000). Protecting, conserving and enhancing critical stream and riparian habitat
and other priority habitats are essential to supporting and recovering threatened and endangered
ﬁsh and wildlife populations throughout the county.

States, counties and other jurisdictions must comply with the federal Endangered Species Act
when species are listed by avoiding harm to any member of the species or the habitat upon which
they depend. County policies and regulations must support recovery of those species. The goal is
to make Clark County a county where sustainable populations of salmon and other native species
are a testimony to a healthy ecosystem; where our well-being is supported by the integrity of the
ecosystem we share with other living species; and where, by ensuring healthy habitat for all
inhabitants of Clark County, we ensure the quality of life we value.

In addition to federally listed species, Clark County also includes populations, or the potential for,
ﬁsh and wildlife species on the Washington State endangered, threatened, or sensitive species list,
as classiﬁed by the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission. The federal status of species under
the Endangered Species Act differs in some cases from state status.In 1998, the state adopted
the Salmon Recovery Strategy (RCW 77.85) as a guide to statewide salmon recovery
efforts. In response, the legislatively established Lower Columbia Fish Recovery Board
(LCFRB) was charged with developing and facilitating implementation of a salmon and
steelhead recovery plan for the lower Columbia River and its tributaries in Washington,
entitled “Washington Lower Columbia Salmon Recovery and Fish & Wildlife Subbasin
Plan” (LCFRB, 2010). The two overarching goals for this plan are to: 1) restore the region’s
ﬁsh species listed as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA) to



E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                          140
                                      CLARK2045
healthy, harvestable levels and 2) protect and enhance other ﬁsh and wildlife species that
have been adversely affected by human actions, including the development and operation
of the Federal Columbia River Power System. In 2013, the National Marine Fisheries
Service (NMFS) adopted the recovery plan as part of the broader “domain plan” that
covers Washington and Oregon tributaries, as well as the mainstem Columbia River and
estuary. The LCFRB and its partners have been actively implementing recovery efforts for
the past 27 years, and its work is guided by a 15-member board that includes
representatives from local governments, the Washington State legislature, the Cowlitz
Indian Tribe, hydropower operators, environmental and landowner interests, and the
public. Clark County holds two seats on the LCFRB, including one County Councilor and
one citizen representative. Clark County has implemented or partnered on
implementation of many projects targeting recovery efforts during this time. Clark County
complies with all local state and federal regulations pertaining to the protection of ESA listed ﬁsh
and wildlife populations during the delivery of capital construction projects. Clark County also
participates in the Regional Road Maintenance ESA Program (Regional Program). The Regional
Program guidelines describe physical, structural and managerial best management practices
designed so that when they are used, singularly or in combination, they reduce road maintenance
activities’ impacts on water and habitat. Participation in the program has resulted in a biological
opinion from NMFS and approval under Limit 10 of the ESA section 4(d) rule.

In addition, land use planning will also accommodate state and federally listed wildlife species
through implementation of the county’s wetlands and ﬁsh and wildlife conservation areas
ordinance and State Environmental Policy Act land use regulations. Protecting and enhancing
critical upland habitat and prioritizing habitat connectivity is essential to supporting and
recovering terrestrial wildlife populations throughout the county.


W A T E R Q U AL I T Y
Clark County has an abundance of streams and groundwater supplies. Groundwater aquifers are
capable of providing huge amounts of water to industry, business, residences and agriculture. The
federal Clean Water Act lists the “beneﬁcial uses” of the United States’ rivers, streams and lakes.
Many beneﬁcial uses are features valued in Clark County and are required to be protected and
restored under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) municipal
stormwater permit. These are:

   •   surface water supply for industrial water supply, agricultural water supply, domestic water
       supply and stock watering;
   •   ﬁsh and wildlife production and habitat, including spawning, rearing, migration and
       harvesting;
   •   recreation and enjoyment, including contact recreation (swimming, wading, etc.), non-
       contact recreation (boating and sport ﬁshing) and aesthetic enjoyment; and



141                                                                    E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
   •   commerce and navigation.

Urbanization inﬂuences stream biological health. The Washington Department of Ecology
Stormwater Management Manual for Western Washington (2024) describes the effects
urbanization has on water bodies. It states that before forests were cleared for farms and towns,
rainfall was largely absorbed into the ground where it replenished streams as springs and seeps.
As settlement occurs, trees are removed and replaced by ﬁelds, buildings and roads. Instead of
soaking into the ground and returning to streams as springs, rainwater runs off rapidly and greatly
increases stream channel erosion and degrades stream habitat. During the summer, stream ﬂow
may be reduced to low levels because less water is available to springs and seeps that feed the
stream. The manual also states that along with changing stream ﬂows, urbanization adds various
pollutants to surface water and groundwater.

The combination of increased runoff and pollutants in stormwater runoff drastically alters stream
habitats. Pesticides washed off landscaped areas can do great harm to aquatic insects that feed
ﬁsh. Stormwater runoff from roads, business, industrial facilities and residences degrades streams
by ﬂushing pollutants that harm ﬁsh and other aquatic life. The volumes of water running off
paved areas also wash away streambed sediments and the creatures that live there. If sediment is
allowed to wash off construction projects and agricultural land, it can smother aquatic creatures in
the streambed, such as smothering salmon eggs. In order to begin to address this problem, a set of
regulations was added to the Clean Water Act in 1987 to decrease problems caused by
stormwater runoff. The Clark County Stormwater Management Program is a direct response to
that mandate since 1999 under Washington Phase I Municipal Stormwater Permits, reissued
every 5 years.

Clark County performs many activities to meet requirements of a Washington Department of
Ecology permit to discharge stormwater to county water bodies and groundwater. The program
contains the following main program elements:

   •   regulatory program for development and redevelopment pollution control;
   •   operation and maintenance of storm sewers and roads to reduce polluted runoff;
   •   inspection of business sites and stormwater facilities for compliance with pollution control
       standards;
   •   watershed planning;
   •   monitoring, data management and evaluation to provide information to manage
       stormwater;
   •   coordination within Clark County and with other permittees;
   •   public involvement and education about untreated stormwater runoff and pollutant
       reduction; and
   •   stormwater capital improvements to reduce the potential harm caused to streams by
       stormwater runoff.




E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                        142
                                    CLARK2045
The regulatory program largely consists of implementing development regulations (CCC Chapter
40.386) requiring stormwater control facilities such as water quality treatment practices,
detention ponds and low impact development practices for development projects. Chapter 40.386
also requires construction projects to minimize erosion and sediment washed into streams from
land development and land-disturbing activities. The water quality ordinance (CCC Chapter
13.26A) addresses pollutants associated with everyday activities such as disposal of used motor
oil and vehicle wash water and mandates all stormwater facilities meet state and county
maintenance standards. In 2012 (and amended every few years, currently 2024 version), the
Department of Ecology published the Stormwater Management Manual for Western Washington,
which provides best available science for stormwater requirements relating to development and
re-development, stormwater maintenance standards and pollution control standards for existing
businesses. The county’s 2013 NPDES municipal stormwater permit required the county to
update its stormwater and erosion control ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.386) and stormwater
manual to be equivalent with the state stormwater manual. The current 2026 county stormwater
manual is equivalent to the Ecology Western Washington manual to implement the state mandate
for development projects to use low impact stormwater facilities where feasible.

The operation and maintenance program involves maintenance and repair of county stormwater
controls such as ponds and grassy swales, cleaning of catch basins and sweeping of roads. The
purpose is to reduce the amount of pollutants discharged from the system and make sure it
operates as designed. The program also includes a program to inspect and ensure that privately
operated stormwater facilities are properly cleaned and maintained. The NPDES stormwater
program also performs stream monitoring and watershed-scale stormwater planning.

Reducing stormwater pollution requires that individuals prevent their homes and businesses from
becoming pollution sources. For that reason, information and education is a major part of the
stormwater program.

Before the late 1990s, large areas of the county were developed without the stormwater control
facilities that prevent pollution and excessive amounts of runoff from harming streams. The
stormwater program includes a program to plan and build stormwater control facilities and stream
restoration projects to address stormwater problems created before the program began in 1999.
The six-year Stormwater Capital Plan is adopted each year by the Clark County Council. The
program maps all existing storm sewer systems and plans to build projects using stormwater fees
from each home, business and government property in unincorporated Clark County.


WETLANDS
Wetlands provide valuable ﬁsh and wildlife habitat and include marshes, swamps, fens and bogs
that perform several other functions. Wetlands can aid hydrology by moderating water overﬂow,
advancing groundwater recharge and enhancing water quality. Water quality is enhanced by
preventing erosion, removing sediments and ﬁltering nutrients and other pollutants from runoff



143                                                                E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                     CLARK2045
and slowing down the ﬂow of water which allows time for pesticides and other chemicals to break
down. Wetlands also provide vegetative habitat and human recreational and open space
amenities.

 Countywide mapping covering the full range of wetland classes is available in a generalized form
through the Clark County Wetland Inventory, the National Wetland Inventory, and hydric soil
mapping; these inventories are inaccurate on a site-speciﬁc basis. More precise wetland
boundaries are not usually known until site speciﬁc analyses are conducted, normally during the
review of individual development proposals. Most wetland areas are in low elevations areas within
relatively close proximity of rivers and streams, or associated ﬂoodplains (Figure 3 and Figure 4).


W E T L A N D S C ON S E R V A T I O N P R O G R A M
The county’s wetland ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.445) was adopted in 1992, signiﬁcantly updated
in 2006, 2014, and most recently 2023. The stated purpose of the ordinance is to:

   •   include best available science as deﬁned in Chapter 365-195 WAC to protect the functions
       and values of wetlands with special consideration to conservation or protection measures
       necessary to preserve or enhance anadromous ﬁsheries;
   •   further the goal of no net loss of functions and values of wetland areas;
   •   encourage restoration and enhancement of wetlands with lower functions and values;
   •   provide greater protection of wetlands with higher functions and values;
   •   are administered with ﬂexibility and attention to site-speciﬁc characteristics;
   •   ensure reasonable use of private property;
   •   do not prohibit development of needed public infrastructure and utilities; and
   •   complement state and federal regulations and programs that protect or conserve water
       quality or ﬁsh and wildlife habitat.

The county recently updated the ordinance in 2023 to reﬂect the best available information as
required by the GMA, more speciﬁcally to reﬂect mitigation sequencing and wetland buffer
protection guidance from the Washington Department of Ecology (WDOE). The ordinance utilizes
the Washington State Wetland Rating System for Western Washington to rate wetlands from
Category 1 to Category 4 based on site speciﬁc characteristics and landscape position. The county
regulates based on a combination of the type of wetland and the intensity of the use around it.
Development proposals involving wetlands often need review by the Army Corps of Engineers
(under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act) and WDOE (under RCWs 90.48 and 90.58).


W E T L A N D S M IT IG A T I O N B AN K IN G
Wetlands mitigation banking is a method of mitigating a decrease in or loss of wetland function by
providing wetland functions and values (e.g. creating, restoring, enhancing and/or protecting
wetlands) away from the site of a proposed development project. A wetland mitigation bank



E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                       144
                                       CLARK2045
generates credits that can be used for wetland mitigation for individual projects with wetland
impacts. Mitigation banking has a number of beneﬁts over other mitigation strategies including:

   •   consolidation of small isolated mitigation projects into larger, more ecologically signiﬁcant
       sites;
   •   higher likelihood of long-term mitigation success; and,
   •   efﬁciency in permit review for projects using bank credits.

Wetland mitigation banking is not a means of reducing the protection and conservation of
wetlands in the urban area. It is only a method to improve mitigation success at a regional scale
and streamline permit review for projects that have wetland impacts. The criteria used to evaluate
and permit wetland impacts are independent of the type of mitigation proposed and, instead,
focus on the beneﬁts and design of the project. A key element to developing an effective wetland
mitigation banking program is to maintain a good inventory of existing and historic wetlands in
order to allow mitigation bank developers to locate sites that are well suited to bank development.
Another key element is to ensure that the wetland permitting process gives due consideration to
the use of mitigation bank credits when they are available. Clark County has a process for
authorizing mitigation banks and actively participates in the Interagency Review Team for wetland
mitigation banks permitted under State and Federal rules in Clark County. There are currently
four wetland mitigation banks operating in Clark County. .


A Q U IF E R R EC H AR G E A R E A S
An aquifer is a body of rock (generally sand, gravel, or fractured basalt in Clark County) that
transmits groundwater in useable quantities to wells. Almost all of the county's industrial water
needs and about 47 percent of public water needs are met by wells located near the Columbia
River, where the overlying deposits consist mostly of coarse sand and gravel. Water inﬁltrates the
soil and percolates through surface rocks into the water Table and then travels deeper downward
into aquifers, which are water sources in most parts of the county. Recharge of aquifers is often
greatly reduced in urban areas because most surfaces are impervious, preventing rainfall from
entering the soil. Some aquifer recharge occurs in urban areas through dry wells and septic system
drain ﬁelds, but these methods may decrease groundwater quality by allowing contaminants to
enter the soil.

Since most of the lowland area of the county is covered with permeable alluvial, or sand, gravel
and silt deposits, there is no one identiﬁable point of recharge. Virtually the entire county pervious
area functions as an aquifer recharge area to some extent. The most critical aquifer recharge areas
are those located near production wells (Figure 6).


A Q U IF E R P R O T EC T I O N P R O G R A MS
Clark County residents and commerce are almost totally dependent on water pumped from
relatively shallow aquifers. Both the quantity and quality of this water is critical. The county has


145                                                                     E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
several programs to protect aquifer recharge amounts and water quality. The stormwater and
erosion control ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.386) for development projects require stormwater
inﬁltration wherever soil conditions make it feasible. This preserves recharge when sites are
covered with buildings and pavement. Stormwater regulations also require that this inﬁltrated
stormwater be treated to remove pollutants.

The water quality ordinance (CCC Chapter 13.26A) prohibits discharging pollutants to surface
water and groundwater. The county implements the ordinance by actively educating businesses
and the public on acceptable ways to manage everyday pollutants such as used oil, paint and dirty
wash water.

The critical aquifer recharge area (CARA) ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.410) identiﬁes critical areas
and places special requirements on higher risk development projects in those areas. The CARA
ordinance was updated in 2005 to reﬂect best available information as required by the GMA and
was most recently amended in 2020.

Source-based policies are typically used to provide protection to larger and less clearly deﬁned
critical areas, such as aquifer recharge areas, or to address other concerns related to ground or
surface water quality. Sewage regulations, particularly those regarding septic system uses, are
administered by Clark County Public Health and are directed toward the protection of critical
areas which are not necessarily at the site of the potential pollutant source. Stormwater
management policies and programs administered by Clark County are similarly intended to
address potential adverse water quality impacts beyond the source site.


FLOOD HAZARD AREAS
Flood hazardous areas are another category of critical area and are often associated with riparian
corridors. Flood hazard areas are deﬁned and delineated by the Federal Emergency Management
Agency (FEMA) to include all areas subject to ﬂooding during 100-year ﬂood events (1 percent-
annual-chance ﬂood event). This deﬁnition encompasses areas along most rivers in the county.
These areas provide wildlife habitat, hydraulic functions, and several additional beneﬁts. Building
limitations in these areas limit damage to persons and property from the periodic ﬂoods (Figure 5).


F L O O D P R O T E C T I O N P R O G R AM S
It is recognized that approximately 90% of all disasters in the US are ﬂood-related. The avoidance
of damage from ﬂooding is accomplished by the application of zoning regulations and building
ordinances. The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) was created by Congress in 1968 and
signiﬁcantly amended in 1973 to:

   •   reduce loss of life and property caused by ﬂooding;
   •   reduce rising disaster relief costs caused by ﬂooding; and
   •   make federally-backed ﬂood insurance coverage available to property owners.


E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                         146
                                      CLARK2045
The program was designed to achieve these goals by:

   •   requiring that new and substantially improved buildings be constructed to resist ﬂood
       damages;
   •   guiding future development away from ﬂood hazard areas;
   •   transferring the costs of ﬂood losses from the American taxpayers to ﬂoodplain property
       owners through ﬂood insurance premiums; and
   •   prohibiting new development in designated ﬂoodways that would aggravate ﬂooding.

The National Flood Insurance Program is a voluntary program based on mutual agreement
between the federal government and the local community. In exchange for adopting and enforcing
a ﬂood plain management ordinance, federally-backed ﬂood insurance is made available to
property owners throughout the community.

The National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 created the Federal Insurance Administration and
directed it to conduct Flood Insurance Studies (FIS) that identify ﬂood-prone areas within the US
and establish and map ﬂood risk zones within those areas. The studies provide technical data for
the adoption of ﬂoodplain management measures required for NFIP participation by a community
and for development of ﬂood-risk information needed to establish ﬂood insurance premiums.

In March of 1977, the county adopted a ﬂood hazard ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.420). Clark
County, in partnership with FEMA, periodically is required to complete updates to the Flood
Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMS) and to Chapter 40.420 . Changes have been made to the ﬂood
hazard ordinance to bring the ordinance into compliance with federal requirements and to comply
with the best available information requirement of the GMA. The ordinance was most recently
amended in 2023.


GEOLOGICALLY HAZARDOUS AREAS
Geologically hazardous areas are not environmentally-valued critical areas such as wetlands or
wildlife habitat, even though many contain critical ﬁsh and wildlife habitat protected by other
ordinances. The primary function of development limitations within geologically hazardous areas
is to limit potential adverse impacts to persons and property. The primary geologically hazardous
areas are those of steep and or unstable slopes, which are often, but not exclusively, found along
the stream corridors.


G E O H A Z A R D P R O T E C T I O N P R O GR A M S
The county’s geologic hazard areas (geohazards) ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.430) was enacted in
1997 and most recently amended in 2019. Maps have been produced showing earthquake
potential and steep slopes with the susceptibility to landslides and erosion (Figures 7, 8 and 9). The
geohazards ordinance was updated in 2005 to reﬂect better seismic hazard vulnerability
information throughout the county and to meet the best available information of the GMA. The


147                                                                    E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                     CLARK2045
county adopted the International Residential Code in 2005. New, more stringent and relevant
seismic codes will be incorporated into the permitting and building ordinances as necessary.


O T H E R H AZ A R D M I T I G A T I O N P R O G R A M S
Natural hazards (such as ﬂoods and landslides, earthquakes, volcano, severe weather, drought,
winter storms and wildﬁres) to Clark County’s natural resources, parklands and other
environmentally critical areas cause millions of dollars of damage every year. In 2016, Clark
Regional Emergency Services Agency (CRESA) lead a multi-agency collaborative effort to create
the Clark Regional Natural Hazard Mitigation Plan (CRNHMP), replacing the previous Multi-
Hazard Mitigation Plan. In 2023 the CRNHMP was updated again. The Federal Emergency
Management Agency (FEMA) approved CRNHMP is designed to be the foundation of a long-term
strategy to reduce disaster losses and break the cycle of damage, reconstruction and repeat
damage. A FEMA approved CRNHMP also makes participating jurisdictions eligible for federal
hazard mitigation grant funds.

As established by the planning partnership, the purpose of the CRNHMP is to deﬁne natural
hazard risk, provide the most up to date information on the identiﬁed hazards, and, through
collaboration and partnerships, establish strategies and actions for reducing the impacts of
disasters in Clark County.

Goals of the plan include:

   •   Reduce and prevent the loss of life and property.
   •   Protect public services and critical facilities from the impacts of natural disasters.
   •   Increase public awareness of vulnerability to natural hazards and educate on risk
       reduction strategies.
   •   Promote community resilience.
   •   Protect environmental resources and utilize natural systems to reduce natural hazard
       impacts.
   •   Develop and implement cost-effective mitigation strategies.

The hazard information contained within the CRNHMP is intended to be integrated into county
and other local jurisdictions’ planning efforts whenever possible. The identiﬁed strategies and
actions within the CRNHMP are of such value they are to be incorporated into the ordinances and
codes of the county wherever possible in order to make natural hazard mitigation a sustainable
part of everyday life.

The inclusion of identiﬁed Hazard Mitigation strategies and action in order to safeguard the
county’s natural resources are an important part of the 20-Year Plan. Whenever possible, the
county and its CRNHMP partners will include proven mitigation strategies and actions as one of
the primary methods of avoiding or lessening damages and impacts from the hazards of future



E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                         148
                                      CLARK2045
natural disasters into the 20-Year Plan and associated plans. The strategies and actions for hazard
mitigation are to be enforceable, sustainable and maintainable for the protection of the land and
its residents.

SHORELINES
The shorelines of rivers, streams and lakes of Clark County are important and sensitive natural
resources and encompass other critical areas such as wildlife areas, wetlands and ﬂood areas.
They provide habitat, drainage, recreational opportunities, transportation and economic
opportunities, some of which may conﬂict with each other. The State Shoreline Management Act
of 1971 (SMA) deﬁnes shorelines as being within 200 feet of the ordinary high water mark or
associated wetlands of all rivers with mean annual ﬂow of 20 cubic feet per second (cfs) or more
and lakes greater than 20 acres in size. This deﬁnition encompasses the majority of shorelines for
most of the rivers and lakes within Clark County, although shorelines of smaller water bodies also
provide many of the same functions.

Clark County’s Shoreline Master Program (SMP) was originally adopted in 1974. The Department
of Ecology issued new shoreline rules in 2003. The county and its cities formed a Shoreline
Coalition in 2008 and applied for an Ecology grant to update SMPs across the county. The county’s
comprehensively updated SMP was approved by Ecology and took effect in September 2012, and
was most recently amended in 2023. Chapter 13 of the Comprehensive Plan contains the county’s
shoreline policies; CCC Section 40.460 contains shoreline development regulations; and the
ofﬁcial shoreline map is in Figure 36.

COLUMBIA RIVER GORGE NATIONAL SCENIC AREA
Clark County contains a variety of scenic areas, typically located near major river systems. The
most prominent is in southeast corner of the county, where approximately 6,000 acres east of the
City of Washougal was designated by Congress as part of the Columbia River Gorge National
Scenic Area (NSA) in 1986. From 1988 to 1996 speciﬁc land use regulations intended to foster the
scenic, natural, cultural and recreational functions of these and other similarly designated areas
within the Gorge were administered by the US Forest Service and an appointed Columbia River
Gorge Commission and staff. In 1996, Clark County adopted an implementing ordinance, which
was deemed consistent with the management plan for the NSA by the Gorge Commission and the
Secretary of Agriculture. This approval allows for county administration and jurisdiction over
these lands.

The Columbia River Gorge Commission approved the revised “Gorge 2020” Management Plan for
the NSA in 2020. In early 2021, the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture concurred with the revisions. As a
result, the county updated its scenic area ordinance (CCC Chapter 40.240) in late 2021. The
Gorge commission reviewed the county’s ordinance for consistency with the management plan in
early 2022 and the county received concurrence from the Secretary of Agriculture in mid-2022.
One of the ongoing efforts in the NSA is a program to improve air quality in the gorge.


149                                                                   E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                       CLARK2045
REGIONAL CONSERVATION & GREENWAY SYSTEMS
Regional Conservation and Greenway Systems are the "resource-based" open space land types
identiﬁed in the Clark County Open Space Commission Final Report (August 1992). The Open
Space Commission identiﬁed 17 functions for open space that were divided into economic,
resource, urban-based and other categories and subsequently identiﬁed a number of "open space
categories" as being of greater importance including the following:

   •   river systems and associated ﬂood plains, which provide low-intensity recreation, natural
       vegetation, shorelines, ﬁsheries and wildlife habitat (for example, the North and East Forks
       of the Lewis River, Lacamas Lake and Creek, Washougal River, Burnt Bridge Creek and
       Salmon Creek);
   •   Columbia River lowlands, providing beneﬁts similar to river systems and ﬂood plains, but
       of a much larger scale than other county river systems;
   •   Cascade foothills, providing signiﬁcant wildlife habitat and vegetation, sensitive water
       features, remote/low intensity recreation; and
   •   dispersed open space areas which are site speciﬁc and combine resource, economic and
       urban based areas.

Conservation and greenway systems may be managed for a variety of uses, depending on the
attributes of the site. Potential uses include wildlife habitat, low impact access for wildlife viewing
and environmental education, regional trails and where appropriate, picnic areas, boat ramps,
ﬁshing areas and regional parks. The Greater Clark Parks District coordinates development of
management scenarios with the state and federal wildlife agencies. Planning for and developing a
park and recreation system which serves the diverse recreational interests of the residents of
Clark County and fosters an environmentally sensitive approach toward preservation and
enhancement of the county's valuable natural resources such as ﬁsh and wildlife habitat, wetlands
and water quality. (See Chapter 7 for more details.)

AIR RESOURCES
Clark County is part of the Vancouver-Portland metropolitan area, which spans both Washington
and Oregon. The airshed is bounded on the south by West Linn, Oregon, on the north by
Woodland, Washington, on the west ﬁrst by the west Portland hills and then further west by the
Coast Range and on the east by the Cascade Mountains. This region experiences a temperate
climate, with mild, wet winters and warm, dry summers. The area's topography, surrounded by
mountains, can contribute to the buildup of air pollutants, especially during certain weather
conditions. Strong atmospheric inversions can lead to stagnant air conditions, increasing the risk
of high pollution levels.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) considers the Vancouver-Portland metropolitan
area to be a single interstate airshed, which is susceptible to elevated air pollution levels,
particularly in areas with dense human activity. The region is particularly vulnerable to air quality



E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                           150
                                     CLARK2045
issues during winter months, when inversions trap pollution near the ground, and in the hotter
summer months when there is a prevalence of wildﬁres.

Wildﬁres have become a major contributor to elevated levels of ﬁne particulate matter (PM2.5) in
the region. Smoke from wildﬁres, both local and from distant areas, can travel long distances and
degrade air quality. These ﬁres can signiﬁcantly increase PM2.5 levels, leading to health concerns
and contribute to the challenges of maintaining air quality during wildﬁre season.

Anthropogenic Sources of Air Pollution: Air pollutants come from a range of sources, which can
be categorized into point sources, area sources, and mobile sources. Each type of source
contributes to overall air quality, but varies signiﬁcantly in terms of emissions and control
measures.

   • Point Sources: These are ﬁxed, stationary facilities like power plants, manufacturing plants,
     and industrial operations. While these sources can generate large volumes of air
     pollutants, emissions from point sources are generally well-controlled through air
     permitting programs, which often require pollution control equipment. Clark County’s
     industrial facilities (major sources) contribute a small proportion of the county’s total air
     pollution, with these sources accounting for less than 5 percent of ozone precursor
     pollutants (such as volatile organic compounds [VOCs] and nitrogen oxides [NOx]) and less
     than 10 percent of ﬁne particulate matter (PM2.5).
   • Area Sources: Area sources include pollution from smaller, dispersed activities such as
     residential wood burning, outdoor burning, use of solvents, and gasoline-powered
     equipment. While each individual source may be small, the collective emissions from these
     sources are signiﬁcant. In Clark County, area sources contribute around 20 percent of the
     total VOCs and NOx and are responsible for most of the PM2.5 air pollution. The largest
     contributor to PM2.5 air pollution is residential wood burning.
   • Mobile Sources: Mobile sources, such as cars, trucks, buses, airplanes, trains, and off-road
     vehicles, are a major source of air pollution in Clark County. As of recent data, mobile
     sources account for over half of the ground-level VOCs and NOx and are responsible for a
     signiﬁcant portion—around 85 percent—of carbon monoxide pollution. They are also a
     small contributor to PM2.5 pollution. While improvements in vehicle emissions technology
     and fuel efﬁciency have helped reduce pollution from this source, mobile sources continue
     to be one of the largest contributors to air quality issues in the region.

Air Quality Maintenance Programs: Clark County has faced challenges in meeting federal air
quality standards in the past, particularly for ozone and carbon monoxide. The area was
designated as a non-attainment zone for ozone and carbon monoxide in 1991 by the Governor of
Washington. In response, the Southwest Clean Air Agency (SWCAA) developed and submitted air
quality maintenance plans to address these pollutants, which included strategies such as reducing
outdoor burning and regulating the use of wood stoves.




151                                                                  E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                       CLARK2045
The implementation of these plans has helped Clark County maintain compliance with federal
standards for ozone and carbon monoxide since the mid-1990s. Carbon monoxide (CO) levels, in
particular, have decreased over time, leading to the removal of the county's CO monitor in 2006.
Under the 2006 CO maintenance plan update, CO monitoring is no longer required as long
as emissions from mobile sources remain below 2002 levels.

However, air quality remains a concern, especially with regard to ozone and ﬁne particulate
matter. Summertime ozone levels have been relatively good in recent years, but the region is still
vulnerable to elevated ozone levels, particularly with rising summer temperatures and as vehicle
miles traveled (VMT) increase and stricter standards are introduced. While Clark County has
historically been in attainment with federal standards, there are still typically several days per year
when air pollution is at unhealthy levels (above the 24 hour average NAAQS standard) in
Vancouver.

Wood Smoke and PM2.5 Pollution: In Clark County, wood smoke is a signiﬁcant source of PM2.5
pollution, especially during the winter when people use wood stoves, ﬁreplaces, and inserts for
heating. Chemical analyses of air samples collected during high PM2.5 days have found that wood
smoke contributes a substantial portion of the pollution on these exceedance days. Recognizing
the impact of wood smoke, the state has implemented programs to encourage the replacement of
older wood stoves with cleaner alternatives. Additionally, outdoor burning within urban growth
areas has been permanently prohibited since 2007 to reduce air pollution.

Wildﬁre smoke contributes additional particulate pollution. As climate change and longer, more
intense wildﬁre seasons have become more prevalent, the frequency and severity of wildﬁre-
related air quality issues have increased. These smoky conditions can persist for days or weeks,
further compromising air quality and public health, particularly for those with respiratory
conditions.

Mobile Sources and Emission Reductions: Mobile sources remain the largest anthropogenic
contributor to air pollution in Clark County, responsible for the majority of emissions of NOx,
VOCs, and carbon monoxide. Mobile sources also contribute signiﬁcantly to greenhouse gas
emissions, which are a growing concern for both air quality and climate change. Efforts to reduce
emissions from mobile sources include stricter vehicle emission standards, improvements in fuel
technology, and incentives for electric vehicle adoption.

The second-largest contributor to air pollution in Clark County is area sources, which account for
about 15 percent of total emissions. The most signiﬁcant component of this category is residential
wood burning, which is responsible for a sizable portion of total air pollution and most of the
wintertime PM2.5 pollution. Industrial emissions follow behind, but industry’s contribution is still
less signiﬁcant compared to transportation and residential wood burning sources. New industries
entering Clark County are required to implement the best available control technology to
minimize emissions.



E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                           152
                                      CLARK2045

Land Use and Transportation Planning: To further improve air quality, land use planning must
incorporate air quality considerations. Decisions regarding zoning, development, and
infrastructure should consider their potential impact on emissions, particularly those related to
transportation and residential heating.

One of the most effective strategies for reducing vehicle-related air pollution is improving
transportation options. Planning for walkable communities, integrated public transportation
systems, and cycling infrastructure can reduce reliance on motor vehicles. Providing convenient
bus routes, bike lanes, and pedestrian pathways for short trips can signiﬁcantly cut down on
emissions from personal vehicles. Connecting bus systems with light rail networks across the
region is a key strategy for improving air quality and reducing congestion.

Air Resources Summary: Ensuring clean air in Clark County requires a multifaceted approach,
involving stricter regulations for mobile sources, better control of area sources like residential
wood burning, and smart land use planning that encourages alternative transportation options. As
Clark County continues to grow, addressing air quality through both regulatory measures and
innovative planning will be crucial for maintaining a healthy environment and ensuring compliance
with federal standards. Additionally, addressing the impact of wildﬁre smoke, which exacerbates
the region's air quality challenges, will be key to improving overall public health outcomes.

GOALS & POLICIES
A variety of programs and policies exist for the protection and conservation of environmentally
critical areas. Due to the geographical overlap of many of the types of critical areas, there is a
functional overlap of many of the policies. A program to address one type of critical area, such as a
building limitation within a ﬂoodplain, may often offer some additional protection for other critical
areas, such as wildlife habitat or wetland functions.



WASHINGTON STATE GOALS & MANDATES
As noted earlier, the GMA requires the identiﬁcation and protection of critical areas (RCW
36.70A.170 and 172). Critical areas can be found within the urban areas and within the rural and
resource areas of the county. These critical areas include: ﬂood hazard areas, geologic hazard
areas, wetlands, shoreline and surface waters, habitat conservation areas, aquifer recharge areas
and scenic areas. Mapped critical areas can be found in Figures 1-11. In addition, the GMA
requires that jurisdictions give special attention to the preservation and enhancement of
anadromous ﬁsheries.

RCW 36.70A.070(9) outlines GMA climate change and resiliency requirements. Chapter 14 –
Climate Element contains most climate change and resilience policies in the Comprehensive Plan,
but other elements also include climate policies. Climate-related goals and policies within this

IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGIES
The following strategies are proposed as a means to achieve the goals and policies of the
Environmental Element. These are a range of strategies that the county is considering and some of
these should be implemented over time.

   •   Develop incentives that encourage open space, recreation and protection of the natural
       environment.


161                                                                   E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT
                                     CLARK2045
  •    Evaluate a variety of funding sources and their feasibility for acquisition of land and other
       programs to implement the policies within the Environmental, Rural and Natural Resource
       Elements.
  •    Develop and implement comprehensive stormwater management plans, including ongoing
       monitoring and funding for all watersheds in the county that comply with recovery
       objectives.
  •    Develop and implement a watershed protection implementation program that is salmon-
       friendly with the goals of resolving and preventing deterioration of all local water
       resources within identiﬁed watersheds. Develop and implement watershed plans that
       recognize watershed processes and that address impacts to wildlife habitat. The program
       shall:
       • protect groundwater;
       • safeguard drinking water quality;
       • protect surface water quality;
       • insure groundwater recharge;
       • control urban ﬂooding;
       • enhance wetland habitat; and
       • establish local funding mechanisms for water quality and water resource protection.
   •   Develop and implement a protocol to identify natural watershed-wide processes, their
       inter-relationships reach by reach and how they might be degraded by human activities.
       The protocol will be designed to associate the watershed processes with the various
       environmental mandates imposed by the state and federal governments on Clark County
       and the jurisdictions within it. The use of a standardized assessment protocol should
       streamline permitting, promote efﬁcient monitoring and focus restoration and mitigation
       projects.
   •   Update ordinances and other regulations to meet salmon recovery goals.
   •   Investigate the use of a Public Beneﬁt Rating System of property taxation to encourage
       development, recording and implementation of Stewardship Plans on parcels essential to
       salmon recovery or other watershed processes.
   •   Develop measures countywide to ensure erosion and sediment control for new
       development, re-development and excavation projects.
   •   Develop regional detention and on-site disposal system.
   •   Adopt the use of land use planning software that analyzes air quality impacts of proposed
       land use actions.
   •   Support educational programs and provide resources for landowners to implement
       wildlife-friendly practices, such as wildlife-friendly fencing or native habitat restoration.
   •   Where necessary, wildlife overpasses or underpasses should be considered to maintain
       connectivity between habitats and allow for animal movement.
   •   The county will do the following to implement its sustainability policy:
       • Lead by example;
       • Encourage innovation in both public and private pursuits;




E NVIRONMENTAL E LEMENT                                                                        162
                                   CLARK2045
      •   Promote and demonstrate efﬁcient and effective use of renewable and consumable
          resources;
      •   Collaborate with public and private partners on projects aimed at sustainability;
      •   Continuously enhance our perspective and expertise in making sustainable choices on
          behalf of the citizens and communities of Clark County; and
      •   Identify and pursue new opportunities that promote sustainable practices.

CHAPTER 5
Transportation Element

INTRODUCTION
The Transportation Element of the Clark County Comprehensive Growth Management Plan
2025-2045 (20-Year Plan) provides the community guiding framework for transportation
investment and priorities over the next 20 years. The Growth Management Act (GMA) requires
that the Transportation Element be prepared to implement, and be consistent with, the Land Use
Element. The Transportation Element helps to ensure that Clark County will be able to
accommodate increased population growth and changes to land use over time, while it also aims to
promote healthy, economically vibrant and livable communities through the development of a
safe, accessible and efﬁcient multimodal transportation system that is not dependent on vehicles
to move people throughout the county.

The Transportation Element identiﬁes speciﬁc transportation projects for the urban and rural
areas of the unincorporated county to improve mobility and roadway safety, as listed in Appendix
A: Transportation Capital Facilities Plan. In addition to identifying projects, the Transportation
Element also recommends various implementation strategies to guide the county in its
participation in regional transportation planning. These implementation strategies provide
guidance on such issues as:

   •   Access management;
   •   Active transportation;
   •   Air quality conformance;
   •   Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) transportation transition plan;
   •   Arterials, highways and transit service multimodal level of service standards;
   •   Freight and goods mobility;
   •   Land use-transportation concurrency;
   •   Transit emphasis corridors;
   •   Transportation Demand Management (TDM) (maximizes the efﬁciency of transportation
       networks by encouraging people to choose options other than driving alone to travel).

Appendix A: Transportation Capital Facilities Plan includes an estimate of expenditures and
revenues associated with implementing recommended transportation improvements. The related
ﬁnancial strategy in Appendix A ensures needed transportation improvements are funded. The
Transportation Element can be amended and supplemented by special studies that later provide
more detailed policy direction and project recommendations. These special studies would




165                                                                 T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
maintain consistency with the countywide Transportation Element, while also qualifying and
reﬁning its recommendations.

GROWTH MANAGEMENT ACT
The Washington State Growth Management Act (GMA) provides legal and policy guidance to the
county regarding preparation of the Transportation Element. The GMA requires a Transportation
Element that implements and is consistent with the Land Use Element of the 20-Year Plan per
RCW 36.70A.070(6). A Transportation Element must include:

   •   Land use assumptions used in estimating and forecasting travel;
   •   Estimated Multimodal Level of Service (MMLOS) impacts to state-owned transportation
       facilities;
   •   Facilities and service needs, including:
       o An inventory of air, water and ground transportation facilities and services;
       o MMLOS standards for all locally owned active transportation facilities, arterials and
           transit routes;
       o MMLOS standards for state owned transportation facilities;
       o Speciﬁc actions and requirements for bringing locally owned transportation facilities
           and services into compliance with the MMLOS standards;
       o Forecasts of multimodal transportation demand and needs for 10 years based on the
           adopted land use plan;
       o Identiﬁcation of state and local transportation system needs to equitably meet current
           and future travel demands; and
       o An ADA transition plan;
   •   Finance, including:
       o An analysis of funding capability to judge identiﬁed system needs against probable
           funding resources;
       o A multi-year ﬁnancing plan that balances needs against available funding; and
       o A discussion of how additional funding will be raised, or land use assumptions
           reassessed to ensure MMLOS standards are met;
   •   Intergovernmental coordination and impact assessment;
   •   Travel Demand-Management (TDM) strategies; and
   •   An active transportation component.

Consistency between the Land Use and Transportation Elements of the 20-Year Plan is of
particular importance. Planned land use must be reﬂected in the travel forecasts to evaluate the
impacts of development. The transportation improvements and implementation measures within
the Transportation Element must adequately support planned land use at adopted MMLOS
standards.

MMLOS standards serve as a tool to gauge performance and help assess the adequacy of the
transportation system, including sidewalks, bicycle lanes, transit and vehicles, and guide the



T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                         166
                                      CLARK2045
current and future improvement projects in the 20-year transportation Capital Facility Plan (CFP)
as listed in Appendix A. These projects are prioritized based on the evaluation criteria in Appendix
A, which relate back to the Goals and Policies found in the 20-Year Plan.

Consistency between the county’s overall Transportation Element, the cities’ comprehensive
plans, the state’s highway system plan, regional transportation plans and transit development
programs, needs to be ensured through intergovernmental coordination. The applicable facilities
and services are those that serve travel needs and have impacts beyond the jurisdiction(s) within
which they are located. The Countywide Planning Policies, noted in the Goals and Policies section
of this chapter, are to provide procedural guidance to the county and cities to help ensure
consistent transportation planning and implementation.


R E L A T I O N T O O T H E R E L E M E N T S O F T H E 20-Y E AR P L AN
The Growth Management Act (GMA) requires that the Transportation Element be implemented
and consistent with other elements of the 20-Year Plan and must include the county’s plan to
ﬁnance identiﬁed local system improvements. The policies and performance standards contained
within this element complement the Land Use Element by providing for transportation needs and
infrastructure in urban centers, addressing the needs of neighborhoods and adapting the rural
transportation system in support of those policies.

Chapter 4 – Environmental Element contains policies related to restoring streams for ﬁsh
passageways and coordination with WSDOT and WDFW to plan and prioritize culvert
replacements to ensure ﬁsh passage barrier removal. Currently, WDFW has identiﬁed 171
county-owned ﬁsh passage barriers. It also includes air quality goals and policies.

Chapter 7 – Parks, Recreation and Open Space Element contains policies related to safe
pedestrian and bicycle routes, and for providing an interconnected network.

Chapter 11 – Community Design Element contains a policy about separating vehicular and
pedestrian circulation using vegetative buffers.

Chapter 14 – Climate Element contains most climate change and resilience policies in the 20-Year
Plan, but other elements also include climate policies. Climate-related goals and policies within
this element are noted in the goals and policies section of this chapter. See Chapter 14 for a
comprehensive discussion of climate policies, some of which overlap with the Transportation
Element.

RCW 36.70A.070(9) outlines GMA climate change and resiliency requirements. The
Transportation Element intersects the requirements of both the resilience and greenhouse gas
emissions reduction sub-element pieces of the Climate Element. Core requirements of the
Climate Element are outlined in Chapter 14 – Climate Element; however, some of the Climate




167                                                                  T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
Element requirements intersect with the Transportation Element. These requirements include the
identiﬁcation of actions that will:

   •   Identify, protect, and enhance community resiliency to climate change impacts, including
       social, economic, and built environment factors, that support adaptation to climate
       impacts consistent with environmental justice.
   •   Result in reductions in overall greenhouse gas emissions generated by transportation and
       land use within the jurisdiction but without increasing greenhouse gas emissions
       elsewhere in the state.
   •   Result in reductions in per capita vehicle miles traveled (VMT) within the jurisdiction but
       without increasing greenhouse gas emissions elsewhere in the state.
   •   Prioritize reductions that beneﬁt overburdened communities to maximize the co-beneﬁts
       of reduced air pollution and environmental justice.


R E L A T I O N S T O O T H E R C O U N T Y P L A N N I N G P O L IC Y D O C U M E N T S
The 20-Year Plan, including the Transportation Element, is part of a hierarchy including the Clark
County countywide planning policies, the Community Framework Plan, the 2010 Clark County
Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan, Clark County zoning ordinance (Title 40, Development Code),
the Clark County Arterial Atlas, the 20-Year Capital Facility Plan, the ADA Transition Plan, and
related implementation documents. The 20-Year Plan, and Transportation Element within, provide
detailed policies for managing growth consistent with the mandates of GMA and the direction of
the Community Framework Plan. Some of the key state, regional and local transportation projects,
programs, plans and studies taken into consideration with development of the Transportation
Element are listed below.

WASHINGTON STATE
   •   The Cascadia High-Speed Rail Study proposes to connect people and communities, increase
       economic competitiveness, and improve quality of life across the Cascadia megaregion.
       This fast, safe, predictable way to travel would connect the metro areas of Vancouver, B.C.,
       Seattle, WA, Portland, OR, and points in between and beyond. Rather than relying on
       congested highways or increasing air trafﬁc, the high-speed rail project offers a sustainable
       alternative to traveling greater distances quickly and reliably.
   •   The Washington Transportation Plan (WTP) is the state’s long-range transportation plan,
       based on the Legislature’s six policy goals: economic vitality, preservation, safety, mobility,
       environmental & health, and stewardship. The related policy plan, 2040 & Beyond, provides
       statewide policy recommendations to the Legislature. The related implementation plan,
       Washington Transportation Plan, Phase 2 – Implementation 2017-2040, applies key policy
       recommendations for the WTP to further develop the state’s complex transportation
       system.
   •   Washington’s 2024 Highway System Plan serves as a vital component of the statewide
       multimodal transportation plan, outlining long-term program needs, ﬁnancing strategies



T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                         168
                                     CLARK2045
      and system improvements. The plan prioritizes the following funding approaches for
      WSDOT facilities as follows:
          o First fund operations maintenance, capital preservation and critical programs such
              as required ﬁsh passage projects and support programs.
          o Then for any remaining funds, $2 should be spent on safety and efﬁciency
              strategies for every $1 spent on highway expansion projects.
  •   Washington’s Strategic Highway Safety Plan: Target Zero is a plan with the goal to reduce the
      number of trafﬁc deaths and serious injuries on Washington’s roadways to zero by the year
      2030. It serves as the state’s Strategic Highway Safety Plan.
  •   The Washington State Active Transportation Plan—2020 and Beyond is a compass for creating
      the future of walking, biking, and rolling on or across state highways in Washington. It is
      used in decisions to help connect people to where they want to go, whether they use active
      transportation for the whole trip or just a part of it, such as walking to a bus stop, riding a
      bike to work, or rolling home from a terminal.
  •   The 2022 Washington State Freight System Plan supports Washington, the second-most
      trade-dependent state per capita in the USA. Washington relies heavily on an efﬁcient
      freight transportation network. In 2022, the freight system supported 1.5 million jobs in
      freight-dependent industries in the state, moving 603 million tons of cargo with an
      estimated value of $707 billion and $212.7 billion in Gross Domestic Product (GPD).
      Freight and goods are shipped into, out of, and around Washington by truck, rail, air,
      pipeline and water. The 2026 Freight System Plan update is underway.

SOUTHWEST WASHINGTON REGION
  •   The Regional Transportation Plan (RTP) for Clark County (2024), prepared by the Southwest
      Washington Regional Transportation Council (RTC), is the region’s principal transportation
      document and provides a complete and up-to-date description of regional transportation
      facilities and issues in the County. The 2024 RTP identiﬁes future regional transportation
      system needs to the year 2045, outlining strategies and improvements necessary to
      maintain adequate mobility within and throughout Clark County and must maintain
      consistency with local plans and policies.
  •   The Regional Safety Action Plan for Clark County, (2023) was developed by RTC to help
      identify transportation focused safety needs and improvements across Clark County. The
      plan takes the Safe System Approach, which acknowledges that deaths and serious injury
      crashes are unacceptable, humans are vulnerable and make mistakes, and that
      transportation networks must be proactive about providing multiple layers of protections
      for all users, whether they travel by foot, car, bike, transit or with the help of a mobility
      device.
  •   C-TRAN’s 2021-2026 Transit Development Plan (TDP) outlines the policy and ﬁnancial basis
      for system operations and facilities.
  •   C-TRAN: 2030 (2016) is a long-range, comprehensive strategy for enhancing public
      transportation for Clark County residents over 20 years. C-TRAN’s plan is designed to
      respond to growing transportation needs and the need to provide expanded, reliable, and
