                                     CLARK2045
       safe service. Maintaining and expanding transit service is vital for ensuring the economic
       vitality and quality of life of the region. C-TRAN: 2045 update is underway.

CLARK COUNTY
   •   The Clark County Bicycle and Pedestrian Master Plan (2010) provides a path to make it safer
       and more convenient for people to get to major destinations in our region on foot or by
       bicycle. The plan identiﬁes ways to improve the transportation network by integrating
       existing sidewalks, bike lanes, and trails. The plan points out that this will require design
       standards that work well with Clark County’s transportation network for motor vehicles.
   •   Clark County Commute Trip Reduction Plan (2025-2029) calls for a reduction in drive-alone
       trips. Increased density and population demand more transit and more multi-modal
       networks. For the transportation system to accommodate more people living in Clark
       County and work efﬁciently and sustainably, we need people to travel by non-drive-alone
       modes, and we need people to live in more dense transit-oriented housing with less
       parking.
   •   Clark County Local Road Safety Plan (2025) identiﬁes trends, roadway risk factors, and
       infrastructure deﬁciencies across the county by analyzing collision data. The plan
       prioritizes high-need locations and recommends low-cost, infrastructure-based
       treatments to reduce fatal and serious-injury collisions. This approach supports a safer and
       more reliable transportation network by directing investments toward the most critical
       safety concerns in Clark County.
   •   The Clark County Parks, Recreation and Open Space Plan (PROST) guides how the county
       cares for and invests in our park system, including trails. Adopted in 2022, this plan is
       updated every 6 years. The 2028-2035 update effort is underway.
   •   Clark County Regional Trails and Bikeways Plan (2006) guides the development and design of
       an interconnected trail and bikeway system within Clark County. The plan primarily
       focuses on shared off road facilities exclusively for non-motorized usage that serve as real
       transportation alternatives, not just recreation.

Standards such as road details, road classiﬁcations and concurrency are included in the
implementing ordinances. The 20-Year Plan is the controlling document and where the
implementing ordinances conﬂict with the 20-Year Plan or fail to implement its policies, the
implementing ordinances shall be amended to be consistent with the 20-Year Plan.

LAND USE ASSUMPTIONS

D E S C R I P T I O N O F H I S T O R I C G R OW T H & D E V E L OP M E N T
Clark County was the fastest-growing county in the state in the 1990s and was second-fastest in
the early 2000s. Between 2010 and 2020, county population grew from 425,363 to 503,311.
During this period, Clark County grew by 77,948 residents or by 18.33 percent.

As of April 1, 2023, the OFM estimates Clark County had an estimated population of 527,400 and
a total of 207,043 housing units. In 2023, the Washington State Employment Security Department
estimated that Clark County had 180,900 jobs.


G R O W T H P R OJ EC T I O N S
The OFM provides counties and cities in Washington state with county-level growth forecasts to
accommodate their planning processes under GMA. The OFM has estimated a population
projection for 2045 ranging from a low of 576,151 to a high of 791,809. The middle series
projection, the one considered most likely by OFM, is 698,416. On May 2, 2023, the County
Council adopted a 2045 population projection of 718,154 to be used for the 20-Year Plan.

On August 8, 2023, the County Council adopted a 2045 employment projection of 269,000 jobs to
be used for the 20-Year Plan. Most employment growth is expected to occur within the
incorporated cities; however, the county will plan for its share of job growth in unincorporated
UGAs and rural areas.

Based on the preferred land use alternative selected on April 28, 2026, the county is responsible
for providing 32,960 housing units and 15,940 jobs in the unincorporated portion of Vancouver’s
UGA and 3,572 housing units and 4,405 jobs in the rural area.

FACILITIES & SERVICES NEEDS

F A C IL I T I E S & S ER V I C E S

The Transportation Element is required to include an inventory of air, water, and ground
transportation facilities and services, including transit alignments, active transportation facilities,
and general aviation airport facilities, to deﬁne existing capital facilities and travel levels to inform
future planning. This inventory must include state-owned transportation facilities within the
county’s jurisdictional boundary. The inventory establishes baseline conditions to serve as a
starting point for the identiﬁcation of current and future system needs.




171                                                                      T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                       CLARK2045
The transportation system in Clark County consists of ﬁve components which keep people and
freight moving throughout the County: airports; marine ports, roadways for motorized vehicles
(cars, trucks, buses and other vehicles); active transportation infrastructure for nonmotorized
facilities serving pedestrians, bicyclists and wheeled mobility users; and rail lines.

AIR TRANSPORTATION
An important example of an economic beneﬁt that can be derived from airports is the ability to
attract compatible land use developments (e.g., commercial or industrial) on or near airport
property. In many instances, land immediately on or adjacent to an airport is ﬂat, easily developed
and relatively inexpensive when compared to more centrally located business district sites.

One of the several requirements of the GMA is that the comprehensive plan of each jurisdiction
should include a process for identifying and siting essential public facilities, including airports and
state and regional transportation facilities, per RCW 36.70A.200.

Local
Publicly owned general aviation airﬁelds within Clark County include Pearson Field and Grove
Field. Pearson Field, located east of downtown Vancouver off SR-14, is operated by the city of
Vancouver and covers 134 acres owned by the National Park Service. Pearson is designated as a
part of the regional transportation system. Grove Field is a Basic Utility Stage I Airport operated
by the Port of Camas-Washougal. Located in the Ferm Prairie area 5 miles north of downtown
Camas, it has a 2,832-foot paved illuminated runway, an above-ground self-fueling station and
hanger space for over 70 aircraft. In addition, Clark County is home to several private airﬁelds.

Regional
Air passenger transportation service for Clark County is primarily provided by the Portland
International Airport (PDX), located in Portland, Oregon, to the southwest of the I-205 Glenn
Jackson Bridge. This is a regional airport with domestic and international passenger and freight
(cargo) service. The sixty-six passenger airlines serving PDX include Air Canada, Alaska Airlines,
America West, American, Condor, Delta, Frontier, Hawaiian, Icelandair, Jet Blue, Pen Air, Sea Port
Airlines, Southwest, Spirit Airlines, United, Virgin America and Volaris. The eight air freight
carriers serving PDX include American Airlines, AmeriFlight, DHL, Empire, Federal Express,
Frontier, Hawaiian, United UPS and Western Air Express. In 2024, PDX reported over 17.5 million
passengers and 200,000 aircraft operations.

WATER (MARINE) TRANSPORTATION
The Columbia River provides a navigable waterway for the Clark County region as part of the
Columbia/Snake River system. Clark County has three port districts, which provide for most of
Clark County’s water transportation services: the Port of Vancouver USA, the Port of Camas-
Washougal and the Port of Ridgeﬁeld. Only the Port of Vancouver serves ocean-going ships and
provides commercial waterborne shipping facilities. Barge trafﬁc operates from the Portland-



T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                           172
                                      CLARK2045
Vancouver metropolitan area to eastern Washington and Oregon. The freight routes are shown in
Figure 5.01: Freight Lines.

Port of Camas-Washougal
The Port of Camas - Washougal provides facilities and services for land, air, water-based
commerce and to enhance employment and recreational opportunities, contributing to the quality
of life in the community. The 430-acre industrial park, located south of SR-14 by Index and 27th to
32nd Streets, was created in 1966 when the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers created a 5.5-mile levee
along the Columbia River. It is home to an average of 48 businesses with approximately 1,000
employees and an annual payroll exceeding $30 million. Steigerwald Commerce Center, the 120+
acres east of the Industrial Park, is the site of future development. The marina has moorage to
accommodate 350-plus boats and a 4-lane launch ramp. The Port district also operates Grove
Field Airport.

Port of Ridgefield
The Port of Ridgeﬁeld is located about 15 miles north of the City of Vancouver. The Port’s taxing
district extends over 57 square miles, and the district is bisected by the I-5 corridor. The Port
adopted the Port of Ridgeﬁeld Comprehensive Plan in 2008. Port owned assets include a 41-acre
site on Lake River, 3 miles from I-5, with a programmed bridge project over the BNSF rail lines to
enable access to 18 acres of land in the 78-acre Ridgeﬁeld Industrial Park located at the southwest
quadrant of I-5 and Pioneer Street. The Port-developed Ridgeﬁeld Industrial Park is now home to
over twenty businesses providing some 800 jobs.

Port of Vancouve r USA
The Port of Vancouver USA is situated at the terminus of the Columbia River’s deep draft channel
and forms a natural gateway to the river-barge ports of eastern Oregon/Washington and northern
Idaho. The Port operates international cargo docks. It is the third-largest port in the state of
Washington. It has ﬁve marine freight terminals, provides 13 deep-draft vessel berths and has two
140-metric ton mobile harbor cranes to enable heavy lift cargo.

The Port is located within 2 miles of I-5 and is also served by the Burlington Northern Santa Fe and
Union Paciﬁc Railroads, the Canadian National and the Canadian Paciﬁc railroads. The Port has
800 acres of developed industrial and marine property with over 50 industrial tenants. Over 2,300
people are directly employed by these businesses and nearly 17,000 jobs are connected to port
activities. The Port has over 500 additional acres of land for future development. Work began in
2004 on the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for this additional land’s
development as part of the Port’s Economic Development & Conservation Plan. The Port’s future
development includes the Columbia Gateway area. The Port focused attention on rail access
improvement with a Simulation and Access Study. The Port is phasing the implementation of the
West Vancouver Freight Access Project.

GROUND TRANSPORTATION

Active Transportation
Active transportation refers to any form of human-powered transportation, including people
walking, using mobility devices, or riding bikes. Active transportation modes include wheelchairs,
assisted mobility devices, two-wheel bikes, cargo bikes, e-bikes, inline skates, scooters, and
skateboards, among others. In addition to providing a low-cost and accessible form of
transportation, active transportation facilities offer many additional beneﬁts to communities that
aim to create an environment where these forms of transportation are convenient, safe and
normal. Active Transportation Facilities are deﬁned in RCW 36.70A.030 as “facilities provided for
the safety and mobility of active transportation users including, but not limited to, trails as deﬁned
in RCW 47.30.005, sidewalks, bike lanes, shared-use paths, and other facilities in the public right-
of-way.”

In 2023, the Washington State Legislature - Joint Transportation Committee found that 30
percent (140,807) of Clark County residents do not drive, yet historically the county has focused
on providing transportation infrastructure for motorized vehicles. 34 This coupled with the large
number of cul-de-sacs, dead end roads and private roads that do not meet public local road
standards make maneuvering around the community in anything other than a motorized vehicle a
challenge.

Bicycle
Existing bicycle facilities on the County’s locally-owned transportation network are mostly
located in the southwestern portion of the county, primarily in Vancouver’s unincorporated UGA,
as shown in Figure 5.02: Existing County Bicycle Facilities. The county-owned network is made up
of a variety of facilities including the following estimates (linear miles):

      •   50 miles of conventional striped bike lanes,
      •   6 miles of paved shared-use paths (in street rights-of-way),
      •   2 miles of buffered bike lanes,
      •   14 miles of paved shoulder facilities, and
      •   258 miles of roadways with no dedicated facility where future facilities are planned.

There is a network of designated bike routes throughout the county. However, they are primarily
on roadways with moderate to high trafﬁc volumes and vehicle speeds that may not be
comfortable and safe for users of all ages and abilities.

Pedestrian
The County’s policy is to construct sidewalks on both sides of the street in Vancouver’s
unincorporated UGA and rural centers, although there are many places in the county where

sidewalks do not exist or the sidewalk is only located on one side of the street. Prior to 1980

The county-owned roadway network in Vancouver’s unincorporated UGA and all rural centers
requires an additional 464 miles of missing sidewalks, including 92 miles of sidewalks on collector
and arterial roadways, to achieve a fully-connected sidewalk network. Missing sidewalks restrict
movement by members of the community with disabilities.

The County is developing an ADA Transition Plan that will identify where the existing sidewalk
facilities do not meet the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) standards and develop a path
towards providing the missing infrastructure. See Appendix L – Americans with Disabilities Act
Transition Plan. Oftentimes the sidewalks are too narrow, include physical barriers, have missing
or non-standard ramps, and lack safe crossings. Table 5.01: Missing Urban Sidewalk Length by
Roadway Classiﬁcation lists the missing urban sidewalk needs for the county-owned network.

The majority of the County’s urban missing sidewalk network, 347.1 linear miles, are on the
County’s local streets that primarily serve residential areas. The local streets should be designed
for all users, including children and those with disabilities, to be able to safely walk, bike, roll, and
access transit. Most local streets are developed and improved by new private development.

New development in rural centers and Vancouver’s unincorporated UGA is required to construct
sidewalks as part of infrastructure improvements. Road modiﬁcation requests, boundary line
adjustments, project phasing and proportionality analysis have allowed development to occur
without providing the needed infrastructure. Historically, ﬁscal accountability associated with
road modiﬁcation decisions has not been part of the county’s decision-making process, and the
cost is transferred to the taxpayers. Figure 5.03: County Missing Sidewalks, shows where the
missing sidewalks are located.

Trails
Beyond bike lanes, there are scattered trail segments, many of which are unpaved, that contribute
to the bicycle infrastructure. A greater portion of the trail infrastructure is available to
pedestrians.

Clark County has a developing system of trails that augment bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure.
Some of the most signiﬁcant regional trails include Burnt Bridge Creek Trail, Columbia River
Renaissance Trail, Discovery Historic Loop, Ellen Davis Trail, Lacamas Heritage Trail, Padden
Parkway Trail and Salmon Creek Trail. While the responsibility for development and maintenance
of these trails is part of the County’s Parks and Nature program, transportation planning efforts
encourage further connectivity through the transportation network.

Transit

Clark County Public Transit Benefit Area Authority (C-TRAN)
C-TRAN is the primary provider of public transit services in Clark County. The agency was formed
by a public vote in 1980 and founded in 1981, and currently serves the municipalities of
Vancouver, Camas, Washougal, Battle Ground, Ridgeﬁeld, La Center, the town of Yacolt and areas
of unincorporated Vancouver. C-TRAN is governed by a nine-member board of directors that
includes three Clark County Councilors, four Council members from the City of Vancouver, and
two members who represent the cities of Battle Ground, Camas, La Center, Ridgeﬁeld, Ridgeﬁeld
and the town of Yacolt.

In 2024, C-TRAN provided 4.97 million rides, continuing an ongoing post-pandemic recovery
trend. C-TRAN’s facilities are shown in Figure 5.04: C-Tran Service Routes and Supporting
Infrastructure.

C-TRAN’s transit infrastructure and services are found in their 2021-2026 Strategic Plan and the
2016 update to C-TAN 2030. C-TRAN is in the process of developing a 2045 vision that includes
numerous new routes that don’t currently exist, plus existing routes with either modiﬁed or
improved service. The vision also includes capital projects on some local routes.

C-TRAN’s existing system includes four transit centers: 1) Fisher’s Landing, 2) Mill Plain, 3) 99th
Street at Stockford Village and 4) Vancouver Mall, as well as nine park-and-ride lots. The park and
ride facilities provide more than 2,200 parking spaces at: 1) Andresen, 2) BPA Ross complex, 3)
Camas/Washougal, 4) Evergreen, 5) Fisher’s Landing Transit Center, 6) La Center, 7) 99th Street
Transit Center at Stockford Village, 8) Ridgeﬁeld and 9) Salmon Creek.

The preliminary ridership number for 2025 is 5,280,313, a 6.3 percent increase from 2024 and the
ﬁrst time since the COVID-19 pandemic that total ridership has exceeded 5 million.

Fixed Route Services
C-TRAN operates seven days a week and holidays to serve the greater Vancouver area. Operating
hours are generally 4:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. on weekdays (with key urban routes operating until
midnight), 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on Saturdays and 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. on Sundays/holidays. C-
TRAN provides ﬁxed route service on 23 local routes operating in Clark County, 2 Bus Rapid
Transit (BRT) routes, and 3 regional express commuter routes between Clark County and
Portland. The two BRT routes, located in the city of Vancouver, represented approximately 37
percent of total ridership. In 2027, the new ‘Vine on Highway 99’, a third BRT route, will provide
more efﬁcient service between downtown Vancouver and the WSU-Vancouver campus in
Vancouver’s unincorporated UGA.

C-TRAN also provides commuter service into TriMet’s downtown Portland transit mall and
connecting service to the MAX light rail system at the Parkrose/Sumner Transit Center off I-205
and the Delta Park – Vanport Transit Center off I-5. These access points allow C-TRAN passengers
to reach destinations in the Portland metropolitan area, including the Portland International
Airport. All C-TRAN routes meet Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility requirements.

Connectors
C-TRAN's Connector provides the cities of Camas, La Center and Ridgeﬁeld with fully accessible
dial-a-ride (reservation-based service) and scheduled stop service (no reservation required) at
designated stops within the service areas. Rides are provided on a ﬁrst-come, ﬁrst-served basis.

Shopping Shuttle
C-TRAN's Shopping Shuttle provides residents of Smith Tower, Lewis & Clark and Columbia House
apartments direct access to major shopping destinations, twice monthly.

Paratransit
C-TRAN's paratransit service, known as C-VAN, meets ADA requirements for complementary
paratransit service. C-VAN provides wheelchair accessible, curb-to-curb services for elderly and
disabled persons who cannot use ﬁxed route services. C-VAN currently operates within the
Vancouver urban growth area (UGA) and within three-quarters-of-a-mile of ﬁxed routes operating
outside the Vancouver UGA.

Cowlitz Indian Tribe

Cowlitz Tribe Transit Service
Cowlitz Tribe Transit Service is a public transit service available to rural residents in South Lewis
(Centralia Amtrak Station) and Cowlitz Counties who live up to 20 miles from the Interstate 5
corridor. Rides include access to life-sustaining and non-life-sustaining medical appointments,
shopping, and cultural or quality-of-life activities.

Expanded Medical Transport
Expanded Medical Transport Program is a public transport program available to rural residents in
Clark, Cowlitz and Lewis Counties who are over the age of 50 and/or individuals with disabilities.
The Expanded Medical Transport Program provides rides north to Chehalis and south to
Vancouver to increase access to medical appointments such as specialty medicine, diagnostic
facilities, cancer treatment centers and hospitals.

Tribal Medicaid Transport
Tribal Medicaid Transport is for Indian Health Services beneﬁciaries and their descendants who
hold a current ProviderOne card and need transportation to medically necessary appointments.
Individuals must live within a 60-mile radius of the Cowlitz Indian Tribe Health Clinic, meet the
Medicaid criteria and have exhausted all other transportation options.

Skamania County Transit
Skamania County Public Transportation provides two transportation programs – Transit and Dial-
a-Ride – both operated by Skamania County Senior Services. The transit bus operates Monday
through Friday (excluding holidays). Buses travel between Stevenson and Carson and the Fisher’s
Landing Transit Center in the city of Vancouver, allowing linkage to C-TRAN and access to the
Portland/Vancouver metro area.

The Dial-a-Ride service is targeted toward seniors, people with disabilities and low-income
people. Rides are coordinated at least 72-hours in advance through the Medicaid Transportation
Broker.

Community in Motion Human Services Council Community in Motion’s Transportation Brokerage
arranges rides for elderly, low income and people with medical needs and disabilities, through
contracts and arrangements with a variety of transportation providers. This service is highly
valued in the community by people that have no access to C-TRAN or C-VAN services or for people
for whom regular transit service does not work.

Rail
There are two mainline rail lines, both owned by Burlington Northern Santa Fe (BNSF) Railway,
that run through Clark County. The mainlines carry both freight and passengers. In addition, the
Lewis and Clark Railway (LINC), also known as the Chelatchie Prairie Railroad, is a 33-mile short-
line railroad owned by, and located entirely within, Clark County. This short-line carries both
freight and recreational passengers on separate portions of the line.

Freight
The BNSF Seattle/Vancouver line is in excellent condition and has 70 to 80 trains operating in the
corridor daily. The BNSF Vancouver/Eastern Washington line is also in excellent condition and
handles about 40 trains daily. Union Paciﬁc Railroad operates some freight trains to Tacoma and
Seattle on BNSF’s lines.



T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                       182
                                     CLARK2045
In 2012, the Lewis and Clark Railway was leased by the Portland Vancouver Junction Railroad
Company (PVJR), a private operator, for the portion of the line from Vancouver Junction to
Heisson. On the lower 14 miles from Rye Junction to Battle Ground, it is anticipated that
considerable freight growth will continue through the freight operator to help support the
economic development vision for Clark County. The upper 19 miles is anticipated for some
possible freight operations and tourism. In 2007, the County was awarded $1.1 million from the
WSDOT Rail Emergent Fund for rehabilitation to the lower 14 miles of track. A new trans-load
facility was created between 78th and 88th Streets. At present, this section of the line serves
freight trafﬁc; no freight trafﬁc exists north of Battle Ground.

Passenger and Recreational
Amtrak has an agreement with BNSF to operate daily passenger service on the freight carrier’s rail
lines. Amtrak trains serve Vancouver daily. During the 1990s, Washington and Oregon began to
invest transportation funds to improve local Amtrak service. In 2024, a total of 126,514
passengers boarded or disembarked at the Vancouver Amtrak station. Amtrak Cascades offers
four daily round trips operating between Seattle and Portland, with two extending to Eugene and
Vancouver, British Columbia. The Coast Starlight provides daily service between Seattle and Los
Angeles via Vancouver and Portland. The Empire Builder train provides daily service between
Chicago and Spokane; one part of the service continues to Seattle while the other part continues,
via Pasco and Bingen-White Salmon, to Vancouver, with service terminating in Portland.

The Paciﬁc Northwest Rail Corridor is one of eleven designated high-speed corridors in the nation.
Its designation pre-qualiﬁes the region for federal high speed rail funding. In late 1995, the
Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) and project partners published
Options for Passenger Rail in the Paciﬁc Northwest Rail Corridor report. An Environmental Impact
Statement on corridor improvements was completed, and construction of rail corridor
improvements began in 1998. Custom-built Talgo trains are now in service on Amtrak’s Paciﬁc
Northwest Rail Corridor service. The Vancouver Amtrak station facility was upgraded as part of
the Eugene to Vancouver B.C. passenger rail service improvements. In the early 2010s, the
Vancouver Rail Project improved safety, reduced rail congestion and improved on-time
performance of Amtrak’s passenger rail service. The project added a new rail bypass track and a
grade-separated crossing over the rail lines for vehicles using west 39th Street in Vancouver.

In 2001, the Lewis and Clark Railroad was leased by the Battle Ground, Yacolt and Chelatchie
Prairie Railroad Association (BYCX), a volunteer group, for the portion of the line from Battle
Ground to Chelatchie, offering recreational excursions from the town of Yacolt to Lucia Falls with
a half-hour stop at Moulton Falls Regional Park. BYCX provides recreational service between May
and December.

Roadway facilities in Clark County consist of a network of Interstate highways, State Routes, and
county and city arterials, collectors and local access streets.

Federal Function Classification
WSDOT deﬁnes functional classiﬁcation as the grouping of highways, roads and streets by the
character of service they provide and was developed for transportation planning purposes. Basic
to this process is the recognition that individual routes do not serve travel independently in any
major way. Rather, most travel involves movement through a network of roads. Comprehensive
transportation planning uses functional classiﬁcation to determine how travel can be channelized
within the network in a logical and efﬁcient manner. The functional classiﬁcation deﬁnes the part
that any route should play in serving the ﬂow of trips through a highway network. WSDOT has the
primary responsibility for developing and updating a statewide highway functional classiﬁcation in
rural and urban areas to determine functional usage of the existing roads and streets for state
routes and non-state route arterials and collectors. Table 5.02: County-Owned Road Miles by
Federal Functional Classiﬁcation, shows the inventory for each classiﬁed roadway type and its
proportional share of the entire roadway system in Clark County, and their locations are shown in
Figure 5.05: County-Owned Roads by Federal Functional Classiﬁcation.

Clark County’s Local Network
Through the Comprehensive Planning process, current and future local arterials are further
categorized using local functional classiﬁcation system—also known as a Comprehensive Plan
Functional Classiﬁcation. Clark County's local arterial functional classiﬁcation system and the
cross-sections for these higher classiﬁed roadways in the county's jurisdiction are provided in the
adopted Clark County Arterial Atlas, in conjunction with the standard detail cross-sections
available in Title 40, the county’s development code. Information provided in the Arterial Atlas for
the county’s arterial roadways represents the county's adopted policy that guides the
development of the future roadway system and deﬁnes the role, function, and design of each
individual roadway to support and implement Comprehensive Plan. The county anticipates
updating the standard detail cross-sections and classiﬁcation system after adoption of the 2025-
2045 Comprehensive Plan, with early discussions contemplating a cooperative effort with the city
of Vancouver to ensure consistency within Vancouver’s unincorporated UGA.

The following provides a brief description of each of Clark County’s roadway Comprehensive Plan
Functional Classiﬁcation.

Urban Parkway Arterial
The Padden Parkway is the only road with this, the highest classiﬁcation within the county’s
functional system. Their purpose of a parkway arterial is to move high volumes of relatively long-
distance trafﬁc speedily across the county or region. Direct land access is prohibited or minimal
and then only to major activity centers of regional impact. Bicycle and pedestrian activity is on a
parallel separated facility.

Urban Principal Arterials
Urban principal arterials (such as NE 78th Street or NE Fourth Plain Road) permit trafﬁc ﬂow
through the urban area and between major elements of the urban area. Principal arterials connect
major trafﬁc generators to other major activity centers and carry a high proportion of the total
urban area travel on a minimum of roadway mileage. They move high volumes of trafﬁc speedily
across the county or region, but with volumes and speeds below those of the principal arterial
parkway classiﬁcation. Access is generally limited to intersections with other arterials and
collectors. Direct land access is minimal and controlled, but less restrictive as compared to
principal arterial parkway. Frequently principal arterials carry important intra-urban as well as
intercity bus routes.

Urban Minor Arterials
Urban minor arterials (such as Hazel Dell Avenue or NE 99th Street) collect and distribute trafﬁc
from principal arterials to streets of lower classiﬁcations or allow for trafﬁc to directly access
destinations. Access to land use activities is generally permitted. They are primarily designed to
accommodate through-trafﬁc but may provide direct access for more intensely developed
properties. Fixed route transit, bicycle and pedestrian activity is moderate.




T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                        186
                                       CLARK2045
Urban Collectors
Urban collectors (such as NE 88th Street) provide land access and trafﬁc circulation within and
between residential neighborhoods and commercial and industrial areas. Collectors do not handle
long through-trips and are not continuous for any great length. Fixed route transit service is low
while bicycling and pedestrian activity ranges from moderate to high.

Urban Local Streets
Most of the county road network is comprised of local streets. Urban local streets provide direct
access to abutting land and access to the higher classiﬁcation facilities. They offer the lowest level
of mobility and usually contain no bus routes. They are not intended to carry through trafﬁc but
make up a large percentage of the total street mileage. New local streets are typically provided as
part of development projects.

Rural Major Collectors
Rural major collectors (e.g. NW 31st Avenue and NE 72nd Avenue) are usually extensions of urban
principal arterials and some urban minor arterials into the rural area. Their primary purpose is to
link rural activity centers with larger towns nearby and to connect them to state arterial routes.

Mostly, they serve intra-county travel. Land access remains subordinate to trafﬁc movement. The
level of ﬁxed route transit, bicycle and pedestrian activity is low.

Rural Minor Collectors
Rural minor collectors (e.g. NE Davis Road and NE Kelly Road) are rural extensions of urban
collectors and some urban minor arterials. They connect rural areas to major collectors and state
routes.

Intersections of Regional Significance
Intersections of regional signiﬁcance are intersections at which at least three (3) approaches have
a comprehensive plan functional classiﬁcation of collector or higher. The intersections of regional
signiﬁcance are listed in Table 5.03: Intersections of Regional Signiﬁcance and shown on Figure
5.06: Intersections of Regional Signiﬁcance. These intersections are evaluated as part of the
concurrency management system. Individual movements at each signalized intersection of
regional signiﬁcance in the unincorporated county shall not exceed an average of two (2) cycle
lengths or two hundred forty (240) seconds of delay, whichever is less.

All unsignalized intersections of regional signiﬁcance in the unincorporated county shall achieve
LOS E standards or better if warrants are not met. If warrants are met, unsignalized intersections
of regional signiﬁcance shall achieve LOS D standards or better.

Washington State Highway System: Interstate and State Routes
In Clark County, there are two interstate highway facilities (I-5 and I-205) and ﬁve state highway
facilities (SR-14, SR-500, SR-501, SR-502, and SR-503) as shown in Figure 5.07: State-Owned
Transportation Facilities. There is also a WSDOT park-and-ride lot at the I-5/Ridgeﬁeld Junction.

Interstate highways are designed to provide for the highest degree of mobility serving large
volumes of long-distance trafﬁc; they are not designed to provide access to land uses. State Routes
serve large volumes of trafﬁc between counties and regions.

I-5
Clark County has a 20.78-mile section of I-5, the major interstate freeway serving the West Coast.
I-5 provides north-south travel and is used for interstate travel from Mexico through California,
Oregon and Washington to the Canadian border. I-5 crosses the Columbia River from Oregon to
Washington over the Interstate Bridge. I-5 has three through lanes in each direction from the
Interstate Bridge north to the Cowlitz County line. Planning partners from WSDOT, ODOT, RTC,
Metro, and the cities of Vancouver and Portland are considering a future replacement of this
bridge.

I-205
Clark County has a 10.57-mile section of I-205, an alternative route to I-5, bypassing the
Portland/Vancouver metropolitan area. I-205 crosses the Columbia River from Oregon to
Washington over the Glenn Jackson Bridge and terminates at I-5 just north of NE 134th Street.
The Glenn Jackson Bridge was opened in 1982 and has four travel lanes in each direction. North of
the bridge, I-205 has three lanes in each direction to a point just north of the interchange with SR
500 where it becomes a two-lane facility in each direction to its terminus.

SR-14
Clark County has a 21.52-mile section of SR-14, the major east-west state highway that extends
from the City of Vancouver east to the I-82 Interchange in eastern Washington. SR-14 runs along
the northern bank of the Columbia River from downtown Vancouver through Clark County to the
Skamania County line. The facility has two lanes in each direction up to milepost 12, and one lane
in each direction across the Camas Slough Bridge. An expanded segment through Camas has two
lanes in each direction.

SR-500
SR-500 is a 22.64-mile facility entirely within Clark County and, for the most part, allows for east-
west cross-county travel. It continues from I-5 east, providing access to the Orchards area, then
traverses rural Clark County until it reaches the Camas urban area. SR-500 intersects SR-14 in
Camas. The facility carries trafﬁc to and from the Clark County regional shopping mall as well as
other signiﬁcant commercial areas and residential communities.




T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                         190
                                      CLARK2045
SR-501
SR-501 is an 11-mile facility entirely within Clark County and extends from the interchange with I-
5 westward with three lanes in each direction along the Mill Plain/15th Street couplet to Columbia
Street. West of Columbia Street the facility is two lanes in each direction. This segment of SR 501
carries trafﬁc to and from the Port of Vancouver USA. The facility reduces to one lane in each
direction, and branches into two in the Vancouver Lake lowlands area with both branches
terminating in the lowlands.

The northern segment of SR-501 was dedicated to the City of Ridgeﬁeld and is no longer a state
highway.

SR-502
SR-502 is a 6.12-mile facility entirely within Clark County and provides the primary east-west
connection between the I-5 and NE 219th Street interchange to Battle Ground where it terminates
at the intersection with SR-503. The facility has two lanes in each direction.

SR-503
Clark County has a 26.58-mile section of SR-503, which provides a north-south connection from
Orchards, through Battle Ground, north into Cowlitz County. The segment of SR-503 between
Fourth Plain Boulevard to the SR-502 intersection in Battle Ground is a facility with two lanes in
each direction. North of SR-502, the SR-503 facility drops down to 1 lane in each direction north
to Cowlitz County.

Highways of Statewide Significance (HSS)
In Clark County, highway facilities deﬁned as “of Statewide Signiﬁcance” are I-5, I-205, SR-14, and
part of SR-501 to access the Port of Vancouver USA. Figure 5.07: State-Owned Transportation
Facilities shows where the HSS facilities are located.

Highways of Regional Significance (HRS)
In the 2024 Clark County Regional Transportation Plan, highway facilities deﬁned as “of Regional
Signiﬁcance” are SR-500, the portion of SR-501 not designated as a Highway of Statewide
Signiﬁcance (HSS), SR-502 and SR-503.

National Highway System (NHS)
In Clark County, the National Highway System includes the Interstate Highway System as well as
other roads important to the nation's economy, defense and mobility. It is designated to focus
federal investment on a set of high-priority routes. Initially, ISTEA required that roads be
designated as National Highway System (NHS) facilities and Congress approved the initial NHS
System with passage of the National Highway System Designation Act of 1995 (NHS Act). Under
Section 1104 of MAP-21 (2012), update and expansion of the NHS was required to additionally
include urban and rural principal arterials that were not included in the NHS before October 1,
2012. This resulted in increasing the NHS in Clark County from about 78.5 centerline road miles


191                                                                  T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
to about 148.5 centerline road miles. Maps of the expanded NHS system, a sub-set of the MTP’s
designated regional transportation system, are available on FHWA’s website.

The NHS includes the Interstate Highway System, as well as other roads important to the nation's
economy, defense, and mobility. It is designed to focus federal investment on a set of high-priority
routes. In 2012, under Section 1104 of the National Highway System Designation Act, the NHS
was expanded to include urban and rural principal arterials. A total of 148.5 road centerline miles
in Clark County are designated NHS routes, as shown in Figure 5.07: State-Owned Transportation
Facilities.

Strategic Highway Network (STRAHNET)
STRAHNET is a system of public highways designated by the Department of Defense and Federal
Highway Administration in collaboration with state Departments of Transportation to
accommodate the emergency transportation of military personnel and equipment in times of
peace and war. This system provides connections to military installations and ports. In Clark
County, I-5 and I-205 are the only STRAHNET highway facilities.

MMLOS S T AN DA R D S F O R C O U N T Y -O W N E D F A C IL I T I E S
The Growth Management Act (GMA) requires local jurisdictions to establish Multimodal Level of
Service (MMLOS) standards for all locally owned arterials, locally and regionally operated transit
routes that serve Urban Growth Areas (UGAs), state owned or operated transit routes that serve
urban areas, if applicable, and active transportation facilities. MMLOS standards represent the
minimum desirable performance level for transportation facilities and services within the region
and serve as a gauge to judge the performance of the overall transportation system. These
standards are used to identify deﬁcient facilities and services in the transportation system for
capital planning and concurrency management.

The forecast needs for county-owned capital facilities are based on the MMLOS selected and
consistent with the growth, densities and distribution of growth anticipated in the Land Use
Element. The forecast should include reasonable assumptions about the effect of any identiﬁed
system management or demand management approaches to preserve capacity or avoid the need
for new facilities.

The GMA deﬁnes concurrency as the requirement that adequate transportation infrastructure is
provided “concurrent with development” to accommodate new growth and offset the impact of
development. This concept allows coordination between the timing of development projects and
transportation improvements such as new streets and intersection improvements. Clark County
and each municipal government therein maintain concurrency programs. Such programs consist of
two key components: a Comprehensive Plan which establishes transportation MMLOS standards,
and an ordinance which deﬁnes the implementation of concurrency requirements.

More about Clark County’s concurrency requirements and management system are found below.

LOCALLY OWNED ARTERIALS
Clark County maintains a local classiﬁcation system as part of the 20-Year Plan. This classiﬁcation
system is reported in the Clark County Arterial Atlas. The Atlas also includes cross-section
drawings for arterial and local street classiﬁcation roads and circulation plans developed as special
studies. When changes are made in the Atlas, they must be part of the annual review process for
the Comprehensive Plan, as the Atlas is a supporting document of the 20-Year Plan.

The GMA states that MMLOS standards shall be established for all locally owned arterials, and
locally and regionally operated transit routes, and active transportation facilities to serve as a
gauge to judge the performance of the system. The GMA directs that these standards should be
established locally and coordinated regionally for local arterials and for highways of regional
signiﬁcance. The standards are used to identify deﬁcient facilities and services in the existing
transportation system. Highways of statewide signiﬁcance have a MMLOS standards set by the
state.




T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                        194
                                             CLARK2045
MMLOS standards can be based on performance along a segment of a roadway or at an
intersection. The Highway Capacity Manual includes different MMLOS deﬁnitions and
descriptions of operating characteristics for freeways, highways, urban streets and signalized
intersections, because driver expectations and the measures of effective performance are
different for each type of facility.

For freeways and highways, LOS is described in terms of the relationship of actual travel speeds to
free-ﬂow speeds, the freedom to maneuver within the trafﬁc stream and the effects of minor
incidents or breakdowns on the trafﬁc stream.

For reference purposes, Table 5.04: Level of Service Generalized Deﬁnitions shows the LOS
deﬁnitions for urban arterials and signalized intersections.

Clark County Council adopted LOS standards for county-owned roadway segments with an
arterial and collector Comprehensive Plan designation that are located within the unincorporated
Vancouver UGA at a volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio that shall not exceed 0.90. These can be seen in
the Arterial Atlas.

The adopted LOS standards for all signalized intersections of regional signiﬁcance is two cycle
lengths, or 240 seconds of delay, whichever is less. All unsignalized intersections of regional
signiﬁcance shall achieve LOS E if warrants are not met, and LOS D if warrants are met.

The v/c ratio measures the actual trafﬁc volume on a roadway relative to its maximum designed
capacity, indicating congestion levels and roadway performance. It is a key metric in trafﬁc
engineering that compares the actual trafﬁc volume on a road or lane to its maximum capacity.

LOCALLY OWNED ACTIVE TRANSPORTATION FACILITIES
The MMLOS standards for active transportation facilities use Level of Trafﬁc Stress (LTS) as a
method to measure the comfort and level of safety that active transportation users feel using a
facility. LTS emerged out of Washington State’s Active Transportation Plan 2020 and Beyond as
the preferred performance metric to grade active transportation facilities. Using LTS as the LOS
indicator for active transportation facilities is in line with WSDOT’s guidance, associated with
WSDOT’s grant funding opportunities and aligned with the state Active Transportation Plan.

In addition to grading facilities, LTS provides guidance to help determine the type of users active
transportation facilities are designed to serve. Figure 5.08: Active Transportation Level of Trafﬁc
Stress Measurement shows how the LTS is measured on a 1-4 scale with Level 1 facilities suitable
for all ages and abilities and Level 4 only used by highly conﬁdent people.

Figure 5.08: Active Transportation Level of Traffic Stress Measurement 45




Within the unincorporated Vancouver UGA, the county’s active transportation infrastructure
MMLOS standard is LTS 2 or better, which is comfortable for most adults.

Within the unincorporated rural area, the MMLOS standard for facilities located on the regional
active transportation network, identiﬁed in the Regional Transportation Plan (RTP), is LTS 3 or
better, which is tolerable for enthusiastic and/or conﬁdent adults.

ACTIVE TRANSPORTATION
Clark County’s planned active transportation network identiﬁes several projects on WSDOT-
owned facilities (state highways). Although the County does not have jurisdiction over these
corridors and would not directly implement the planned active transportation facilities, County
staff can use the network when coordinating with WSDOT to advocate for their implementation.

In 2022, the Washington State Legislature added a complete streets requirement to RCW
47.04.035, ensuring that WSDOT incorporates these principles as part of state highway
improvements. Consistent with WSDOT’s Active Transportation Plan, 2020 and Beyond, the
complete streets projects aim to provide active transportation facilities that achieve LTS 2 or
better. WSDOT has a state mandate to ultimately provide LTS 2 (comfortable for most adults) or
better active transportation facilities on Highways of Regional Signiﬁcance while prioritizing the
implementation of facilities within population centers throughout the county. Therefore, the
County’s active transportation network provides connectivity with the mandated state facilities.

PAST TRENDS AND EXISTING DEMAND
The nature of transportation demand is inﬂuenced by numerous demographic, economic, and
sociological factors. Clark County has experienced signiﬁcant housing and employment growth in

recent years, with population and employment both increasing by approximately 23 percent
between 2010 and 2023. Employment growth has been characterized by an increase in high-tech
and retail employment, particularly in the suburban areas. The increasingly dispersed employment
tends to add to automobile travel demand and creates challenges for public transit service.

Demographic Trends
The nature of transportation demand is inﬂuenced by numerous demographic, economic, and
sociological factors. Clark County has experienced signiﬁcant housing and employment growth in
recent years, with population and employment both increasing by approximately 23 percent
between 2010 and 2023. Employment growth has been characterized by an increase in high-tech
and retail employment, particularly in the suburban areas of Clark County. The increasingly
dispersed employment tends to add to automobile travel demand and creates challenges for
public transit services. The share of residents aged 65 years and older has increased from 11.7
percent in 2010 to 17.1 percent in 2023. Housing density has trended up in Clark County, with the
share of single-family residences decreasing from 77 percent in 2000 to 72 percent in 2023.

Commuting T rends
The rise of work-from-home employment after the COVID-19 pandemic, including both fully
remote and hybrid work arrangements, has signiﬁcantly shifted commute travel patterns in Clark
County and throughout the United States. The share of work-from-home employees in Clark
County increased from 5.7 percent in 2010 to 18.7 percent in 2023, a 222 percent increase.

and Commuter Trends, 2010-2023.

By using both HPMS and Streetlight data sources, the county can track estimated VMT in two
different ways. HPMS provides trafﬁc counts along roadway segments and is a dataset with many
years of past data and a stable collection methodology, which provides stability for tracking small
changes over time. Streetlight data can provide more granular data, including travel behavior for
multiple travel modes, as well as demographic and socioeconomic insights. However, this data
source is proprietary and more likely to change over time. Even small changes in methodology
could make it difﬁcult to compare changes in travel behavior over time.

VMT per capita information provides a baseline for the VMT reduction policies in Chapter 5 –
Transportation Element and Chapter 14 – Climate Element. Continued coordination with the
Regional Transportation Council (RTC) and cities on pursuing a regional VMT reduction
monitoring methodology in alignment with Washington State Department of Transportation
guidance is planned for the future.

Please see Chapter 14 – Climate Element for greenhouse gas emissions data related to the
transportation sector.

FORECASTING FUTURE DEMAND
The forecast covers at least ten years based on the adopted land use plan to inform the
development of a Transportation Element that balances transportation system safety and
convenience to accommodate all users of the transportation system to safely, reliably, and
efﬁciently provide access and mobility to people and goods. Priority must be given to inclusion of
transportation facilities and services providing the greatest multimodal safety beneﬁt to each
category of roadway users for the context and speed of the facility.

Travel demand forecasts were developed by Regional Transportation Council (RTC) staff using the
2024 Regional Transportation Plan (RTP) regional travel demand model. The travel demand model
network assumes construction of transportation improvement projects identiﬁed in the adopted
2024 RTP 6-year and 20-year project lists. Model results were analyzed for the preferred
alternative adopted by County Council on April 28, 2026, to identify street segments (links) and
intersections where transportation improvements beyond those identiﬁed in the RTP may be
necessary.



52
     Source: 2022 Streetlight data provided by WA Department of Commerce.


203                                                                           T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                      CLARK2045
By 2045, Clark County is anticipated to accommodate a total population of 718,154 and
employment of 269,000. In the regional transportation planning process, long-range housing and
employment growth forecasts are spatially allocated into Transportation Analysis Zones (TAZs),
then converted to trip generation forecasts. Clark County is represented by 665 TAZs in the
regional travel demand model managed by METRO in partnership with RTC.

The Regional Travel Forecasting Model for Clark County is used as a tool to analyze existing and
future transportation system performance. It is speciﬁcally used to forecast model uses
demographic data as a basis for travel forecasts with the basis for the 2045 travel demand forecast
model being the underlying forecast of 2045 land uses. Travel model process involves trip
generation, trip distribution, mode split and trip assignment to the regional transportation system.

Population and employment growth require a combination of expansion of public facilities and
services as well as land use planning to provide safe, accessible, and reliable access between
homes and jobs throughout the region via a variety of modes. Between 2025 and 2045, the
regional travel demand model forecasts a 52-53 percent increase in weekday daily person trips,
resulting in an average of 2.67 to 2.69 million weekday daily person trips by 2045. The regional
transportation highway system is anticipated to include a 1.3 percent increase in highway lane
miles and an approximately 26 percent increase in transit service hours by 2045.

Land use forecasts indicate signiﬁcant growth for suburban areas within Clark County. This
internal growth is anticipated to reduce the proportion of trips which cross the Columbia River
daily. In 2010, 87 percent of trips remained in Clark County with 13 percent going into Oregon. By
2045, the share of trips remaining in Clark County is anticipated to increase to approximately 93
percent.

The Growth Management Act (GMA) requires that transportation system improvements be put in
place concurrently with land development. An extensive list of capital improvements has been
included in the 2024 RTP to address the wide array of transportation needs for the Clark County
region as expressed through the comprehensive planning efforts of its jurisdictions. The projects
include roadway improvements, trafﬁc signals, road widenings, overlays, intersection
reconstruction, access ramps, bicycle lanes and sidewalks, school crossings, guard rails, culvert
replacements, and storm drainage improvements. The total for the regional transportation
infrastructure needed to accommodate growth over the next 20 years will require an investment
of approximately $4.83 billion in maintenance and preservation costs and $4.48 billion in capital
improvement costs in addition to the estimated $6 billion Interstate Bridge Replacement program.

   •   The preferred alternative raises the volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio to 0.904 for the I-5

The preferred land use alternative results in a lower number of person trips, vehicle miles traveled
(VMT), vehicle hours traveled (VHT), and vehicle-hours of delay than the 2016 comprehensive
plan. The preferred alternative results in approximately 3,000 fewer daily bridge crossings. This
will result in lower levels of congestion at and near the Columbia River crossings.

The preferred land use alternative results in several congested (v/c > 0.90) lane-miles of roadway.
However, the lower overall vehicle delay indicates these impacts will be relatively localized.

The reduced level of congestion and fewer bridge crossings suggests a higher degree of balance
between housing and employment due to City- and County-initiated land use actions. Providing
viable employment opportunities in closer proximity to housing creates a higher likelihood of
shorter trips and increased opportunities for non-single-occupancy vehicle trips, including transit
and active transportation trips.

The RTP includes a series of improvement projects on I-205 between the Columbia River crossing
and the Padden Parkway to improve capacity and connectivity. These include improvements to the
NE 134th Street/Salmon Creek and Padden Parkway interchanges as well as new auxiliary lanes
from SR-500 to Padden Parkway. The RTP travel demand model indicates that some congestion
will remain on NE 88th Street, with PM peak hour volumes exceeding capacity of the planned I-
205 northbound off-ramp at NE 72nd Avenue.

The RTP identiﬁes several long-range improvement projects along the SR-503 corridor between
Fourth Plain Boulevard in Vancouver and SR-502 in Battle Ground, including additional travel
lanes, access management, and a grade-separated interchange at Padden Parkway. The SR-503
corridor serves planned growth in the Battle Ground and Vancouver UGAs as well as being a major
travel route for rural commuters. The corridor will operate well assuming completion of the RTP
project list.

ACTIVE TRANSPORTATION
Systemwide active transportation mode share will be similar for all alternatives. The upzoning in
the preferred land use alternative may provide greater opportunities for active transportation
commute, shopping, and other trips. In addition, provision of higher-density population and
employment centers will reduce the cost of providing active transportation facilities to connect
major trip generators.

Congestion on major corridors could serve to encourage pedestrian and bicycle trips for shorter
non-work trips and bicycle work trips, if active transportation facilities are provided at a safe level.

FREIGHT
The movement of freight is critical to the economic health of Clark County, Southwest Washington
and the Portland metropolitan region. Signiﬁcant improvements to the freight rail system would
be necessary to reduce the existing bottlenecks and increase system capacity.

The Washington State Transportation Commission 2007 Statewide Rail Capacity and System
Needs Study indicated that rail capacity is not keeping pace with growth in demand and identiﬁed
a list of project and policy recommendations to better accommodate freight rail needs in Clark
County.

Truck freight mobility is dependent on roadway trafﬁc operations. Two indicators of freight
performance are total vehicle hours of delay and PM peak hour roadway v/c ratio. The number of
PM peak hour delays for the preferred land use alternative is 744 hours. The preferred alternative
results in a slightly higher number of lane-miles of congested roadway (14.18 miles) than existing
conditions (11.57 miles) during the weekday PM peak hour, suggesting that while total delay will
decrease, congestion will be spread across a greater portion of the transportation network. To
some extent, the impact of increased PM peak hour congestion on freight movement may be
partially mitigated by truck shipments shifting to off-peak hours to avoid periods of peak
congestion.

TRANSIT
Increased zoning density and expansion of UGAs based on the preferred land use alternative will
improve the utility of public transit in those areas and reduce the cost of providing transit services
and facilities to connect major trip generators. C-TRAN may need to expand service hours in areas
with increased development density, but the additional service would be focused primarily within
existing UGAs.

Increased transit ridership might be gained through provision of additional park-and-ride facilities
to capture commuter work trips on I-5, I-205 and other regional facilities. Development of these
park-and-ride facilities would require signiﬁcant capital expenditure and increased operating
expenditure. Delays on I-5 and I-205 may serve to inhibit transit ridership.

The 2024 RTP six-year project list includes development of a new BRT corridor on Highway 99
from the Vancouver waterfront to the WSU-Vancouver campus as well as an extension of the
existing BRT Fourth Plain Boulevard corridor from Vancouver Mall Transit Center to the Mill Plain
Transit Center.

The expansion of high-capacity transit corridors with BRT service will encourage transit usage. On
local routes and cross-river commuter routes, C-TRAN buses will operate in mixed trafﬁc with
relatively higher delays, disincentivizing transit ridership. Increased ridership might be gained
through provision of additional park-and-ride facilities to capture commuter work trips on I-5, I-
205 and other regional facilities. Development of these park-and-ride facilities would require
signiﬁcant capital expenditure and increased operating expenditure.

ADDITIONAL ACTIONS & CONSIDERATIONS TO ADDRESS FUTURE
NEEDS

Aging Readiness
Clark County is anticipating rapid growth in its population of older residents. By 2040, 25 percent
of county residents will be 65 and older, up from 16.4 percent in 2020. Clark County proactively
developed the Aging Readiness Plan (ARP), which was updated in 2023. The ARP recognizes that
people are working to create communities that are good places to live, work, grow up and age in.
Affordable and appropriate housing, supportive community features and services, and
transportation options help create places where everyone can live independently and participate
in civic and social life as they age. Recommendations within this plan focus on connectivity of




54
     Source: Regional Transportation Model, RTC




209                                                                       T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                       CLARK2045
missing public infrastructure, support for social services, and zoning and planning standards that
encourage age-friendly communities that older adults can thrive in.

Carbon Re ducti on / Climate Change / Green Transportation
The Washington State Transportation Carbon Reduction Strategy (TCRS) builds upon the 2021
State Energy Strategy. The TCRS describes the policy framework Washington State is using to
reduce transportation emissions and identiﬁes the types of strategic actions Washington is
investing in to work toward achieving the state statutory Greenhouse Gas emissions limits. The
TCRS serves as an implementation tool for the Federal Highway Administration’s Carbon
Reduction Program, an educational tool, and to support future planning efforts by establishing a
baseline for decarbonization actions across the state.

Washington State and METRO have adopted Comprehensive Climate Action Plans (CCAP),
developed through the Environmental Protection Agency Climate Pollution Reduction Grants.
Washington’s plan includes four transportation strategies. METRO’s plan also includes
transportation actions.

Traditionally, green transportation efforts have focused on the development of active
transportation infrastructure, such as sidewalks, bike lanes and transit stops. Increasingly, and in
step with advances in technology, policy has sought to support zero- or low- greenhouse gas
emissions.

The following are some of the additional infrastructure needs to support the reduction in
greenhouse gas emissions.

   •   Electric Vehicle (EV) infrastructure as part of private development as well as in the public
       rights-of-way.
   •   Short-term bicycle parking infrastructure at key destinations such as parks, schools, park-
       and-ride facilities, retail and government buildings.
   •   Safe pedestrian crossings at key destinations such as parks, schools, transit stops, retail
       and government buildings.
   •   Connectivity for the active transportation infrastructure, such as providing key sections of
       missing sidewalks and bike lanes that serve parks, schools, transit stops, retail and
       government buildings.

Several funding programs focus on providing these types of missing infrastructure improvements.
Partnerships with related service providers, such as C-TRAN and adjacent municipalities, are key
to enhancing county grant applications and opportunities for collaborative projects.

Climate-related severe weather events pose an immediate and long-term threat to the reliability
and capacity of the transportation network. Continued and enhanced system maintenance,
repairs and preservation will increase the resiliency of regional infrastructure.




T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                         210
                                     CLARK2045
Additional information can be found in Chapter 14 – Climate Element.

Commute Trip Reduction
A Commute Trip Reduction (CTR) law was ﬁrst passed by the state legislature in 1991 followed by
an updated law, the CRT Efﬁciency Act in 2006. The CRT Efﬁciency Act modiﬁed the scope of the
CRT program to ensure that CRT plans and employer goals are coordinated with transportation
and growth plans and focus on urban growth areas with the most congested state highways.
Under the CRT Efﬁciency Act, local jurisdictions were allowed to create Growth and
Transportation Efﬁciency Centers (GTECs) to obtain funding and ﬂexibility in implementing
programs. The Act also expanded the role of WSDOT and Regional Transportation Planning
Organizations (RTPOs) in CRT planning.

The overall statewide goals of the CTR program are to: 1) improve transportation system
efﬁciency; 2) conserve energy; and 3) improve air quality. The program requires participation by
the state’s largest employers; those with over 100 employees arriving at work between 6 AM and
9 AM year-round and located in area of Washington most affected by trafﬁc congestion. In Clark
County there are four CTR affected jurisdictions:

   1.   Vancouver;
   2.   Camas;
   3.   Washougal; and
   4.   Unincorporated Clark County (UGA).

In October 2007, the RTC Board approved CTR Plans for each of these four jurisdictions. The
implementation process requires that local jurisdictions, Regional Transportation Planning
Organizations (RTPOs), major employers, transit agencies, WSDOT and the CTR Board work
collaboratively. In 2015, local and regional CTR Plans were updated and submitted to the CTR
Board with a speciﬁc focus on setting the future Plan’s CTR goals and targets. In compliance with
the Washington State Commute Trip Reduction Law, Clark County offers several elements in our
Commute Trip Reduction (CTR) program:

   •    An on-site Employee Transportation Coordinator (ETC);
   •    Guaranteed/Emergency Ride Home;
   •    Promotion of the Clark County Commute Trip Reduction website and online ride-matching
        service; and
   •    Promotion of CTR campaign events.

The Clark County Commute Trip Reduction Website, www.ClarkCommute.org, is loaded with
information on travel options for commuting to work. It offers a commute tracker tool that
enables you to track your work commute and calculate your savings when you choose an
alternative commute to work.

                                       CLARK2045
Complete Streets
In 2019, Clark County adopted a complete streets program, which is designed to provide street
and road designs that incorporate safe access for all potential users, including individuals with
disabilities, bicyclists, pedestrians, transit users and motorists. Clark County deﬁnes Complete
Streets as a transportation system that supports multiple uses, is more conductive to public life
and the efﬁcient movement of people along streets designed primarily to move automobiles and
trucks and is designed to allow active and ample space for pedestrians, bicycles and transit and
safe and convenient travel along streets/roadways for all users. Users is deﬁned as including, but
not limited to, persons of all ages and abilities, including children, youth, families, older adults,
individuals with disabilities, pedestrians, bicyclists, commercial vehicles, delivery/service
personnel, motor vehicle drivers, transit users and drivers, emergency service providers, freight
and adjacent land users.

The Complete Streets standards are found in CCC 40.350.010 are consistent with the Clark
County Standard Details Manual and CCC 40.350.015 and .030.

To reduce reliance on automobiles, Clark County needs to develop adequate sidewalks and
bikeways to access activity centers and allow people to safely and easily get to their destinations.
Developing complete streets with active transportation infrastructure is a strategy that can
maximize the existing transportation system’s capacity by reducing the number of vehicles
contributing to congestion and air quality issues.

As the majority of roads constructed in the county are provided by the development community in
conjunction with development permits, it is important to note that their past reliance on road
modiﬁcations to reduce project costs has come at the expense of the community-wide active
transportation network as cross-circulation and frontage improvements are often waived. with
little consideration, if any, of the adopted Comprehensive Plan goals and policies.

Environ menta l Justice
While the County’s transportation system provides important infrastructure for moving people
and goods throughout the county, heavy trafﬁc on roadways places signiﬁcant impacts on the
community. The Washington State Department of Health Environmental Health Disparities map
(see Figure 37 in Appendix B) shows communities experiencing a disproportionate share of
environmental health burdens based on 25 indicators of environmental exposures, environmental
effects, socioeconomic factors, and sensitive populations. In Clark County, the most vulnerable
communities are often located in proximity to heavy trafﬁc roadways experiencing negative
impacts from poor air quality and other environmental hazards.

Maintenance and Preservation
Climate-related severe weather events pose an immediate and long-term threat to the reliability
and capacity of the transportation network. Continued and enhanced system maintenance,




T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT                                                                          212
                                       CLARK2045
repairs and preservation will increase the resiliency of regional infrastructure and, over time, will
reduce the ﬁnancial obligation of providing a comprehensive transportation system.

Neighborhood Tra nsportation Manag ement P rogram
In May 2025, County Council approved a Neighborhood Trafﬁc Management Program (NTMP) to
address safety concerns on local streets such as speeding, cut-through trafﬁc, and
pedestrian/bicycle hazards. This program was approved with dedicated staff and funding and was
designed as an annual program where the community submits requests, the county reviews
applications and selects the projects to move forward, the county then designs and implements,
weather permitting, all in a single calendar year. Some smaller projects may extend into the next
calendar year due to unforeseen circumstances and some larger projects due to their complexity.

This program will enable more people to move around the community without being dependent on
motor vehicles. It increases the safety of local streets, which often serve parks and schools.

Safety
The frequency, severity, location and type of crashes are assessed by WSDOT and the county.
There are several safety plans that help the county identify where the safety issues are located on
the County’s transportation system. This includes looking at motor vehicle and active
transportation safety issues.

Target Zero, the Washington State Strategic Highway Safety Plan: Target Zero (SHSP) was developed
to identify Washington’s trafﬁc safety needs and to guide investment decisions in order to achieve
signiﬁcant reductions in trafﬁc fatalities and serious injuries. Priority areas include pedestrians
and bicyclists, and the older driver age threshold has been lowered from 75 to 70 because data
shows risk factors for older drivers have a statistically signiﬁcant break point at age 70.

RTC instituted quarterly reporting of fatality and serious collisions within the RTC region. The
reports are provided to the Board of Directors. Technical committees use the latest data available
from the WSDOT Crash Data Portal. The county monitors accidents on the county-owned
transportation system.

Speed Ma nagemen t
Roadway speed plays a role in how safe the transportation system is for all users based on
WSDOT’s Level of Trafﬁc Stress (LTS) level of service standard as shown in Figure 5.08: Active
Transportation Level of Trafﬁc Stress Measurement. Reducing roadway speeds can also reduce the
cost of providing safe active transportation infrastructure. The County’s current approach for
setting speed is not standardized, and it considers the existing development conditions over the
projected densities. Therefore, transportation infrastructure may be developed that meets the
needs of today but then have to be redeveloped to address future needs based on full build-out of
the preferred alternative land use plan. This increases the County’s long-term costs.




213                                                                    T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                     CLARK2045
Transporta tion De mand Ma nagement
Transportation Demand Management (TDM) is about reducing auto trips, shortening some trips
and eliminating others that are unnecessary. TDM is a strategy to maximize the existing
transportation system’s efﬁciency. Common TDM strategies are transit use, carpooling,
vanpooling, working ﬂexible hours/compressed schedule, and remote work. TDM can also include
getting users to mode shift into walking or biking.

Vehicle Miles Trav eled
Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) is the measure of all the miles traveled by motor vehicles on the
transportation system. It is a helpful measure of system use and tailpipe greenhouse gas
emissions. Resources are directed to actions that help improve performance and reduce
greenhouse gas emissions.

Per capita VMT means the number of miles traveled using cars and light trucks in a calendar year
divided by the number of residents in Washington. The calculation of this value excludes vehicle
miles driven conveying freight.

HB 1181 (2023) encourages efﬁcient multimodal transportation systems that will reduce
greenhouse gas emissions and per capita vehicle miles traveled. VMT reduction efforts are
increased through a number of funding programs such as the Commute Trip Reduction program,
Complete Streets program and Mitigation and Air Quality improvement program. The Washington
State Department of Commerce shall compile, maintain, and publish a summary of the per capital
VMT annually in the unincorporated portions of each county.

and trafﬁc volumes. Additional planning assumptions were then applied to further revise the
network and develop the proposed active transportation network. Figure 5.11: Proposed Active

ADA T R AN S I T I O N P L A N
The Transportation Element is required to include a transition plan for transportation as required
in Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990. As a necessary step to a program
access plan to provide accessibility under the ADA, state and local government, public entities, and
public agencies are required to perform self-evaluations of their current facilities, relative to
accessibility requirements of the ADA. The agencies are then required to develop a transition plan
to address any deﬁciencies. See Appendix L – Americans with Disabilities Act Transition Plan. The
plan is intended to achieve the following:

   •   Identify physical obstacles that limit the accessibility of facilities to individuals with
       disabilities;
   •   Describe the methods to be used to make the facilities accessible;
   •   Provide a schedule for making the access modiﬁcations; and
   •   Identify the public ofﬁcials responsible for implementation of the transition plan.

the county to fund planned transportation improvements, including active transportation needs.

CONCURRENCY

C O N C U R R E N C Y R E Q U I R E M EN T S
The concurrency requirement of the GMA mandates that local jurisdictions adopt and enforce
ordinances that prohibit development approval if the development causes the LOS on certain
transportation facilities to decline below the standards adopted under the comprehensive plan,
unless transportation improvements or strategies to accommodate impacts of the development
are made concurrent with the development. Concurrently with development means that
improvements or strategies are in place at the time of development, or that a ﬁnancial
commitment is in place to complete the improvements or strategies within six years. Clark County
will meet these requirements through implementation of the adopted concurrency ordinance.

Concurrency policies are applied to local arterials identiﬁed in the capital facilities plan. Highways
of statewide signiﬁcance are exempt from local policies. The concurrency requirements of the
GMA closely match the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) short-term impact analysis
requirements as they both evaluate transportation impacts (namely the roadway, corridor and
intersection LOS) at the year of opening of the development or a speciﬁed short-term analysis
year. A SEPA transportation impact analysis would specify a study area. Concurrency requires an
evaluation of area-wide impacts and speciﬁc mitigation of those impacts concurrent with the
development opening.


217                                                                     T RANSPORTATION E LEMENT
                                     CLARK2045
CONCURRENCY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
The concurrency management system must address concurrency monitoring and concurrency
regulation for new development. The county and its cities are responsible for concurrency
monitoring, and the project applicant is responsible for demonstrating concurrency of the
proposed development. The concurrency management system will include all designated corridors
along identiﬁed arterials and their intersections on the regional system, except for facilities of
statewide signiﬁcance or intersections with facilities of statewide signiﬁcance. In addition, all
intersections of regional signiﬁcance will also be subject to concurrency testing. Implementation
of concurrency monitoring in the county and with local jurisdictions consists of the following
strategies:

   •   LOS is monitored in an established database that includes all intersections within the
       concurrency management system;
   •   The regional model and other trafﬁc simulation models are used to estimate LOS for
       roadway segments. A trafﬁc data collection program has been established for roadway
       segments; and
   •   A tracking system is in place to monitor development applications for “used capacity;” and
       reserved capacity for new development is based on approved applications.

Any changes made to CCC 40.350.020 must conform to this chapter and Appendix A:
Transportation Capital Facilities Plan.
